description: Design a solar photovoltaic system from resource assessment through energy yield modeling and financial analysis, covering module selection, string sizing, inverter optimization, and loss chain quantification.

steps.description: Characterize the solar resource at a site using TMY data, converting global horizontal irradiance (GHI) to plane-of-array (POA) irradiance through transposition models, and quantifying shading losses from horizon profiles and nearby obstructions.

inputs.name: site-coordinates
inputs.desc: Latitude and longitude of the project site

inputs.name: tmy-data-source
inputs.desc: Typical Meteorological Year dataset (NSRDB, Meteonorm, SolarAnywhere) with GHI, DNI, DHI, temperature, wind speed

outputs.name: poa-irradiance-profile
outputs.desc: Monthly and annual POA irradiance in kWh/m2 for the selected tilt and azimuth, with shading loss factors applied

outputs.name: site-thermal-profile
outputs.desc: Ambient temperature distribution and wind speed statistics for cell temperature modeling

process: Obtain TMY data for the site. Compare at least two data sources (NSRDB and Meteonorm) and use the lower P50 value unless site-specific ground measurements exist for correlation.

Select array tilt and azimuth. For fixed-tilt, start with latitude tilt for annual optimization or latitude minus 10-15 degrees for summer-peaking loads. For trackers, model single-axis horizontal with backtracking.
Apply a transposition model to convert GHI/DNI/DHI to POA irradiance. Use the Perez model for accuracy or Hay-Davies as a simpler alternative. The choice affects annual yield by 1-3%.

Build a horizon profile from site survey or lidar data. Calculate row-to-row shading loss from the ground coverage ratio (GCR). For fixed-tilt, GCR of 0.35-0.45 balances energy density with shading loss.

Quantify the site thermal profile. Cell temperature follows the Sandia or NOCT model: Tcell = Tamb + (NOCT - 20)/800 x POA. Higher wind speeds reduce cell temperature. This feeds the temperature derate in yield modeling.

steps.description: Select PV modules based on technology trade-offs and size strings to match inverter MPPT voltage windows across the full operating temperature range.

inputs.name: poa-irradiance-profile
inputs.desc: Monthly and annual POA irradiance with shading factors

inputs.name: site-thermal-profile
inputs.desc: Temperature distribution for voltage calculations

outputs.name: module-selection
outputs.desc: Selected module with datasheet parameters: Pmax, Voc, Vmp, Isc, Imp, temperature coefficients, degradation rate, and bifacial gain if applicable

outputs.name: string-configuration
outputs.desc: Number of modules per string and strings per inverter MPPT, with voltage range verification at temperature extremes

process: Compare module technologies. Mono PERC is the baseline. TOPCon offers 0.5-1% higher efficiency with better temperature coefficient. HJT has the best temperature coefficient (about -0.26%/C vs -0.35%/C for PERC) but higher cost. Bifacial adds 5-15% energy gain depending on albedo and mounting height.

Calculate string length from inverter MPPT voltage window. At the coldest expected temperature (record low or ASHRAE 99.6% design temperature), Voc must not exceed the inverter maximum input voltage. Use: Voc_cold = Voc_STC x (1 + TempCoeff_Voc x (Tmin - 25)).

At the hottest expected temperature (ASHRAE 0.4% design temperature), Vmp must stay above the inverter MPPT minimum voltage. Use: Vmp_hot = Vmp_STC x (1 + TempCoeff_Vmp x (Tmax_cell - 25)), where Tmax_cell includes irradiance heating above ambient.
The maximum string length is floor(Vmax_inverter / Voc_cold). The minimum string length is ceil(Vmppt_min / Vmp_hot). If min exceeds max, the module-inverter pairing does not work at this site.

Select the string length that keeps the operating voltage near the middle of the MPPT window for the majority of operating hours. Longer strings reduce BOS cost (fewer strings, combiner boxes, home runs) but reduce design flexibility.

steps.description: Select inverter topology and optimize the DC/AC ratio to maximize energy harvest while managing clipping losses against cost savings.

inputs.name: module-selection
inputs.desc: Selected module parameters

inputs.name: string-configuration
inputs.desc: String length and count per MPPT

outputs.name: inverter-specification
outputs.desc: Inverter model, rated AC power, MPPT channels, efficiency curve, and grid-code compliance features

outputs.name: dc-ac-ratio
outputs.desc: Installed DC capacity divided by inverter AC rating, with annual clipping loss quantified

process: Choose inverter topology. Central inverters (500kW-4MW) minimize cost per watt for utility scale. String inverters (50-350kW) allow per-string MPPT and eliminate DC combiner boxes. Microinverters serve residential but add per-module cost and communication complexity.

Size the DC/AC ratio (also called inverter loading ratio or ILR). For a fixed-tilt system in a moderate resource, ILR of 1.2-1.3 is typical. Higher ILR (1.3-1.5) suits tracker systems or sites where marginal DC capacity is cheap relative to inverter and interconnection cost.

Quantify clipping loss. Run an hourly simulation: for each hour where DC power exceeds AC rating, the inverter clips to rated AC. Annual clipping loss of 1-3% is generally economic. Beyond 3-4%, the marginal module adds cost without proportional energy.

Verify inverter efficiency across the operating range. CEC-weighted efficiency (which weights partial-load hours more heavily than peak) matters more than peak efficiency. A 98.5% CEC vs 98.0% CEC inverter recovers the efficiency difference over the project life.

Confirm grid-code compliance features: reactive power capability (typically +/- 0.85 power factor), voltage ride-through, frequency ride-through, ramp rate control, and anti-islanding per IEEE 1547-2018 Category III for utility-scale.

steps.description: Build a complete energy yield model quantifying every loss in the chain from incident irradiance to metered AC energy, following PVsyst methodology for bankability.

inputs.name: inverter-specification
inputs.desc: Inverter model and efficiency curve

inputs.name: dc-ac-ratio
inputs.desc: ILR and clipping loss estimate

outputs.name: annual-energy-yield
outputs.desc: P50 and P90 annual energy production in MWh with full loss tree breakdown

outputs.name: loss-chain-breakdown
outputs.desc: Each loss category quantified: soiling, shading, temperature, mismatch, wiring, inverter, transformer, clipping, availability, degradation

process: Start from POA irradiance. Apply the incidence angle modifier (IAM) loss: at off-normal angles, reflection from the glass surface reduces absorbed irradiance. Physical models use the Fresnel equations; empirical models use ASHRAE or Martin-Ruiz correlations. Typical annual IAM loss is 2-4%.

Apply spectral correction if using a model that accounts for it. Air mass and precipitable water vapor shift the solar spectrum relative to the STC reference (AM1.5). This matters more for CdTe (spectral gain at high air mass) than crystalline silicon.

Apply soiling loss. Site-specific soiling rates range from 1% per month in dusty arid climates to 0.1% per month in wet climates. Cleaning schedule reduces the average soiling loss. Model soiling as a sawtooth: linear accumulation between cleaning events.

Calculate cell temperature hourly from ambient temperature, wind speed, and irradiance. Apply the temperature derate: Pdc = Pstc x (1 + gamma x (Tcell - 25)), where gamma is the temperature coefficient of power (negative, typically -0.35 to -0.45%/C for crystalline silicon).

Apply remaining DC losses: module mismatch (1-2%), DC wiring (1-2%), module LID/LeTID (0.5-1.5% first year), and nameplate tolerance (use median from flash test data if available). Then apply inverter efficiency from the efficiency curve at each operating point, transformer loss (typically 0.5-1%), and AC wiring loss. Sum losses to get net AC energy. Express results as P50 (median year) and P90 (exceeded 90% of years, accounting for interannual irradiance variability, typically 5-7% sigma).

steps.description: Build the financial model for a PV project: LCOE calculation, PPA pricing, degradation-adjusted cash flows, and sensitivity analysis on key variables.

inputs.name: annual-energy-yield
inputs.desc: P50 and P90 energy production estimates

inputs.name: loss-chain-breakdown
inputs.desc: Itemized losses for cost-benefit analysis of mitigation measures

outputs.name: lcoe-analysis
outputs.desc: Levelized cost of energy in $/MWh with all-in cost assumptions and degradation schedule

outputs.name: project-economics
outputs.desc: IRR, NPV, payback period, DSCR at P90, and sensitivity tornado chart on key variables

process: Calculate LCOE: total lifecycle cost (capex + NPV of opex + NPV of inverter replacement + decommissioning) divided by NPV of lifetime energy production. Use a real discount rate (nominal minus inflation). Typical utility-scale LCOE components: modules 25-35%, inverters 5-8%, BOS 20-30%, soft costs 15-25%, O&M NPV 10-15%.

Build the degradation schedule. Year 1 degradation (LID + initial settling) is typically 2-3%. Subsequent annual degradation is 0.4-0.6% per year for crystalline silicon. Bifacial modules may degrade slightly faster on the rear side. The degradation rate is the single largest uncertainty in 25-35 year production estimates.

Model PPA pricing. The PPA price must cover debt service (DSCR of 1.3-1.4x at P90 energy for investment-grade financing), equity return (levered IRR target, typically 8-12%), and O&M escalation. PPA escalators of 1-2% per year are common but reduce competitiveness against flat PPAs.

Run sensitivity analysis. The variables with the largest impact on IRR are typically: energy yield (+/- 5%), capex (+/- 10%), PPA price (+/- $5/MWh), degradation rate (+/- 0.1%/yr), and discount rate (+/- 1%). Present results as a tornado chart showing IRR sensitivity to each variable independently.

Assess bankability risk factors. Lenders evaluate: technology risk (module warranty, inverter replacement schedule), resource risk (P90 vs P50 spread), curtailment risk (grid constraints), offtaker credit quality, and insurance coverage. The gap between P50 and P90 energy directly determines the debt sizing.

description: Design a battery energy storage system from cell chemistry selection through pack architecture, BMS design, thermal management, and degradation modeling to safety certification.

steps.description: Select battery cell chemistry and form factor by matching application requirements to electrochemical trade-offs in energy density, cycle life, safety, and cost.

inputs.name: application-requirements
inputs.desc: Power rating (MW), energy capacity (MWh), duration, cycle count target, operating temperature range, and safety constraints

inputs.name: project-constraints
inputs.desc: Space envelope, weight limits, budget targets, supply chain preferences, and regulatory requirements

outputs.name: cell-selection
outputs.desc: Selected cell with chemistry, form factor, capacity, voltage, cycle life curve, and calendar aging parameters

outputs.name: chemistry-trade-off-matrix
outputs.desc: Comparison of candidate chemistries across energy density, cycle life, safety, cost per kWh, temperature range, and supply chain risk

process: Map the application to a chemistry class. LFP (lithium iron phosphate) for long cycle life (3,000-6,000 cycles to 80% SOH at 1C), superior thermal stability (no thermal runaway below 270C), and lower cost per cycle. NMC (nickel manganese cobalt) for higher energy density (200-270 Wh/kg vs 120-160 Wh/kg for LFP) where space or weight is constrained. Sodium-ion for cost-sensitive, moderate-cycle applications where energy density is less critical.

Select form factor. Prismatic cells (50-300Ah) simplify pack assembly and thermal management. Cylindrical cells (21700, 46800) offer better cycle life consistency and easier thermal management per cell but require more complex module assembly. Pouch cells maximize packing density but require external compression for cycle life.

Evaluate cell-level specifications. Capacity, nominal voltage, internal resistance (DC-IR), rate capability (continuous and pulse C-rate), and temperature range. Request cycle life data at the expected depth of discharge (DOD) and C-rate, not just the headline 1C/100% DOD number.

Assess safety certifications. Cells should pass UN 38.3 for transport, UL 1973 for stationary storage, and IEC 62619. Request abuse test results: nail penetration, overcharge, external short circuit, crush, and thermal abuse at the cell level.

Evaluate supply chain. Lead time, minimum order quantity, manufacturing location, and bankability (Tier 1 status from BloombergNEF or equivalent). For large projects, negotiate cell-level warranties including capacity fade guarantees (typically 60-70% of nameplate after stated cycle count) and defect rate limits.

steps.description: Design the battery pack from cell-level up: series/parallel configuration to hit voltage and capacity targets, busbar routing, fusing strategy, and contactors.

inputs.name: cell-selection
inputs.desc: Cell chemistry, capacity, voltage, internal resistance

inputs.name: chemistry-trade-off-matrix
inputs.desc: Trade-off data for design margin decisions

outputs.name: pack-architecture
outputs.desc: Series and parallel cell count, module grouping, voltage range (min to max SOC), total energy capacity, and peak power capability

outputs.name: electrical-design
outputs.desc: Busbar sizing, fuse ratings, contactor selection, pre-charge circuit design, and isolation monitoring approach

process: Determine the series count from the target DC bus voltage. For grid-scale inverters, 1000V or 1500V DC bus is standard. Series cells = Vbus_target / Vcell_nominal. Verify that Vmax (fully charged, cold temperature) does not exceed inverter maximum input voltage, and Vmin (discharged, hot temperature) stays above inverter MPPT minimum.

Determine the parallel count from the energy or power requirement. Parallel strings = Energy_target / (Series_count x Vcell_nominal x Ccell). Verify that peak current per cell at maximum power does not exceed the cell's rated continuous or pulse C-rate.

Design the module structure. Group cells into modules (typically 12-24 series cells per module) for manufacturing, maintenance, and safety isolation. Each module gets its own cell monitoring circuit (voltage and temperature sensors per cell or cell group). Module-level fusing allows isolation of a failed module without taking down the rack.

Size the busbars for maximum continuous current with a temperature rise limit (typically 30C above ambient). Use copper for low resistance; aluminum for weight savings. Calculate I2R losses across the full busbar path and include them in the efficiency model. Add pre-charge resistor and contactor to limit inrush current when connecting the pack to the DC bus.

Design the isolation monitoring system. Battery packs in grid-scale applications must maintain galvanic isolation from ground. An isolation monitoring device (IMD) continuously measures resistance between DC bus and ground, triggering an alarm or disconnect below the threshold (typically 100 ohm/V).

steps.description: Design the battery management system: cell monitoring, SOC estimation, balancing strategy, protection logic, and communication architecture.

inputs.name: pack-architecture
inputs.desc: Series/parallel count, module structure

inputs.name: electrical-design
inputs.desc: Voltage range, current limits, fusing and contactor layout

outputs.name: bms-specification
outputs.desc: BMS architecture with cell monitoring accuracy, SOC estimation method, balancing approach, protection thresholds, and communication protocols

outputs.name: protection-logic
outputs.desc: Overvoltage, undervoltage, overcurrent, overtemperature thresholds and response actions with timing

process: Define the BMS architecture. Distributed BMS places a cell monitoring IC on each module (measuring cell voltages and temperatures) communicating to a central controller via daisy-chain (isoSPI, CAN, or proprietary). Centralized BMS routes all cell connections to one board, limiting scalability but reducing cost for small packs.

Specify cell voltage measurement accuracy. For LFP, the flat voltage curve demands accuracy better than +/-3mV to distinguish SOC in the 20-80% range. For NMC, +/-5mV is adequate. Synchronous measurement across all cells is needed for accurate balancing decisions.

Implement SOC estimation. Coulomb counting (current integration) drifts over time. OCV lookup works only at rest. A Kalman filter or equivalent observer combines both: use the OCV-SOC curve as the measurement model and coulomb counting as the state transition model, with the internal resistance providing an additional observable. Recalibrate at full charge and full discharge rest periods.

Design the balancing strategy. Passive balancing (bleeding excess charge through resistors) is simple and cheap but wastes energy and generates heat. Active balancing (shuttling charge between cells via switched capacitors or transformers) preserves energy but adds cost and complexity. For grid-scale LFP, passive balancing at 50-200mA per cell is the standard approach. Run balancing during rest periods to avoid affecting SOC estimation.

Define protection thresholds and response timing. Overvoltage: disconnect charge path within 1 second if any cell exceeds Vmax (e.g., 3.65V for LFP). Undervoltage: disconnect discharge path if any cell drops below Vmin (e.g., 2.5V for LFP). Overcurrent: immediate disconnect for short circuit (hardware comparator, not software), timed disconnect for sustained overload. Overtemperature: reduce power above 45C cell temperature, disconnect above 55C.

steps.description: Design the thermal management system for the battery pack: heat generation modeling, cooling system sizing, thermal runaway propagation prevention, and thermal testing methodology.

inputs.name: bms-specification
inputs.desc: Operating parameters, balancing heat load, protection thresholds

inputs.name: protection-logic
inputs.desc: Temperature thresholds that define cooling system capacity requirements

outputs.name: thermal-system-design
outputs.desc: Cooling method, coolant loop sizing, air flow requirements, insulation strategy, and thermal runaway propagation mitigation

outputs.name: thermal-model-results
outputs.desc: Maximum cell temperature at rated power, temperature gradient across pack, and thermal time constant for transient events

process: Calculate heat generation. Cell heat comes from I2R losses (ohmic heating from internal resistance) and reversible entropic heating. At 1C continuous, total heat is approximately I2 x Rinternal per cell. For a 280Ah LFP cell at 0.3 milliohm, thats about 23W per cell at 1C. Multiply by cell count for pack-level heat load. Add BMS electronics, contactor, and busbar losses.

Select cooling method. Air cooling is simplest (fan-forced air through channels between cells) but limited to about 1-2 kW/m2 heat removal. Liquid cooling (glycol-water through cold plates or bottom cooling) handles 5-10 kW/m2 and provides tighter temperature control (+/-2C across pack vs +/-5C for air). Immersion cooling in dielectric fluid offers the highest heat transfer but adds cost and complexity. For grid-scale at 0.5C-1C average, air cooling often suffices. For high-power applications (2C+), liquid cooling is necessary.

Size the cooling system. The coolant flow rate follows from: Q = m_dot x Cp x delta_T, where Q is heat load, Cp is specific heat of coolant, and delta_T is allowable coolant temperature rise (typically 5-10C). Size the heat exchanger to reject this heat to ambient at the hottest design day. Include a chiller if ambient temperature plus delta_T exceeds the cell temperature limit.

Design thermal runaway propagation prevention. Even if cell-level thermal runaway cannot be prevented in all cases, pack-level propagation must be stopped. Strategies: thermal barriers between cells (mica sheets, aerogel blankets, intumescent materials), vent gas management (direct venting to outside through fire-rated ducts), and spacing between modules. Test to UL 9540A: trigger thermal runaway in one cell and verify no propagation to adjacent cells within 24 hours.

Validate with thermal testing. Instrument a representative module with thermocouples on cell surfaces and between cells. Run it at rated power in a thermal chamber at the design ambient temperature. Verify that cell temperatures stay within the operating window and that the temperature gradient across the module matches the model prediction within 3C.

steps.description: Model battery degradation from calendar aging and cycle aging mechanisms, size the overbuild for end-of-life capacity, and structure the warranty to match project economics.

inputs.name: thermal-system-design
inputs.desc: Operating temperature profile that affects degradation rate

inputs.name: thermal-model-results
inputs.desc: Cell temperature distribution under various operating profiles

outputs.name: degradation-forecast
outputs.desc: Year-by-year capacity fade and resistance growth with overbuild recommendation to meet end-of-life energy guarantee

outputs.name: warranty-structure
outputs.desc: Warranted capacity at each year, throughput limits, temperature and DOD operating envelope for warranty validity

process: Model calendar aging. Calendar aging depends on temperature and SOC (state of charge at rest). Higher temperature and higher resting SOC accelerate SEI layer growth. For LFP at 25C and 50% SOC, calendar aging is approximately 1-2% per year. Each 10C increase roughly doubles the rate (Arrhenius relationship). Store batteries at 30-50% SOC when not cycling to minimize calendar loss.

Model cycle aging. Cycle aging depends on depth of discharge, C-rate, and temperature. Deeper cycles cause more capacity loss per cycle but deliver more energy per cycle, so the loss per MWh throughput is often similar across DOD ranges. Use the manufacturer's cycle life curve (capacity vs cycle count at specified DOD and temperature) and convert to an equivalent full-cycle count for the expected usage profile using rainflow counting.

Combine calendar and cycle aging. The total capacity fade is approximately the sum of calendar fade and cycle fade (linear superposition works as a first approximation for the first 80% of life, though degradation accelerates as it approaches the knee of the aging curve). Build a year-by-year model using the expected cycling profile (cycles per day, average DOD, average temperature from the thermal model).

Size the overbuild. If the project requires delivering 100 MWh at year 15, and the degradation model predicts 78% remaining capacity at year 15, install 100/0.78 = 128 MWh nameplate. This overbuild is the largest single driver of BESS capital cost. Reducing operating temperature by 5C or narrowing the DOD window by 10% can reduce required overbuild by 5-10%.

Structure the warranty. Manufacturer warranties typically guarantee a minimum remaining capacity (e.g., 60% at 10 years or a stated throughput in MWh). Define the operating envelope that preserves warranty validity: maximum cell temperature, maximum C-rate, DOD limits, and cumulative throughput. The project's BESS controller must enforce these limits. Include augmentation rights (ability to add cells or modules to restore capacity at a known price) in the contract.

description: Engineer the grid interconnection for a generation or storage project from initial study through protection coordination, power quality compliance, and commissioning testing.

steps.description: Navigate the utility interconnection study process: feasibility, system impact, and facilities study, identifying upgrade costs and schedule risks at each stage.

inputs.name: project-parameters
inputs.desc: Generation type, nameplate capacity (MW), location, point of interconnection, requested interconnection service (energy resource or network resource)

inputs.name: utility-territory
inputs.desc: Utility or ISO/RTO, applicable interconnection procedures (FERC LGIP/SGIP or state equivalent), queue position if applicable

outputs.name: study-results-summary
outputs.desc: Feasibility findings, system impact study results (thermal, voltage, stability, short circuit), and facilities study cost estimate with network upgrade allocation

outputs.name: interconnection-risks
outputs.desc: Identified risks: queue position dependencies, cluster study cost allocation, upgrade cost exposure, and schedule to commercial operation

process: Submit the interconnection request with the required deposit and technical data. For FERC-jurisdictional queues, this enters the cluster study process. Provide accurate data: nameplate MW, power factor range, reactive power capability, fault current contribution, and proposed point of interconnection.

Feasibility study (30-45 days typical): screens for obvious thermal overloads and voltage violations at the POI. A pass here does not guarantee interconnection; it means no fatal flaw at the screening level. A fail identifies which facilities need reinforcement.

System impact study (6-12 months for cluster studies): models the project along with all other projects in the same cluster. Evaluates steady-state thermal loading, voltage regulation, transient stability, and short circuit duty. Network upgrades identified here are allocated across projects in the cluster based on the utility's methodology (often pro-rata by MW or by the 'but-for' test).

Facilities study (3-6 months): provides the detailed engineering scope and cost estimate for the interconnection facilities (gen-tie line, interconnection substation, utility metering, and allocated network upgrades). Review the cost estimate against the project's pro forma. Network upgrade costs that exceed the project's budget typically require renegotiation or withdrawal.

Execute the interconnection agreement. Key terms: milestone schedule (financial security, construction start, commercial operation), default and termination provisions, cost responsibility for upgrades, and operating requirements (reactive power, frequency response, ride-through obligations). Missing milestones can result in queue loss.

steps.description: Perform power flow and short circuit studies to verify the project's impact on the grid and ensure equipment ratings are adequate.

inputs.name: study-results-summary
inputs.desc: Utility study findings and identified constraints

inputs.name: interconnection-risks
inputs.desc: Specific risks requiring detailed engineering analysis

outputs.name: power-flow-results
outputs.desc: Voltage profile, thermal loading, and reactive power requirements at the POI under normal and contingency conditions

outputs.name: short-circuit-analysis
outputs.desc: Three-phase and single-line-to-ground fault current contribution from the project, and total fault duty at the POI

process: Build or obtain the power system model. Use PSS/E, PSCAD, or PowerWorld with the utility's base case. Add the project's generator model (for inverter-based resources, use the WECC second-generation or manufacturer-specific models). Include all other projects in the queue cluster.

Run power flow for the key dispatch scenarios: peak load with project at full output, light load with project at full output, and peak load with project offline. Check thermal loading on all circuits between the POI and the first strong bus. Verify voltage at the POI stays within ANSI C84.1 Range A (0.95-1.05 pu) under all scenarios.

Analyze contingency cases (N-1 at minimum). Simulate the loss of each transmission element between the POI and the bulk system. Verify that the project can ride through the contingency without voltage collapse and that remaining elements do not exceed emergency thermal ratings.

Calculate short circuit contribution. Inverter-based resources contribute 1.1-1.2 times rated current during a fault (limited by inverter current capability), unlike synchronous machines that contribute 5-10 times rated current. Model the inverter's fault current response per IEEE 2800. Verify that total fault duty at the POI does not exceed the interrupting rating of existing breakers.

Determine reactive power requirements. IEEE 1547-2018 Category III requires the project to provide dynamic reactive power support. Size the inverter's reactive power capability to maintain power factor at the POI as specified in the interconnection agreement (typically +/- 0.95 or better). If the inverter cannot meet the requirement alone, evaluate static VAR compensators or synchronous condensers.

steps.description: Design the protection system for the interconnection: relay selection, coordination with utility relays, and anti-islanding detection.

inputs.name: power-flow-results
inputs.desc: Normal and contingency operating conditions at the POI

inputs.name: short-circuit-analysis
inputs.desc: Fault current levels for relay setting calculations

outputs.name: protection-scheme
outputs.desc: Relay types, settings, and coordination study showing time-current curves and operating sequences

outputs.name: anti-islanding-design
outputs.desc: Islanding detection method, detection time, and trip logic

process: Define the protection zones. At minimum: generator zone (between the inverter and the step-up transformer), interconnection zone (between the step-up transformer and the POI), and the utility line zone (utility-owned relays on their side of the POI). Each zone requires primary and backup protection.

Select relays for the generator zone. Overcurrent (50/51), overvoltage and undervoltage (27/59), overfrequency and underfrequency (81O/81U), and reverse power (32) are the minimum set. For inverter-based resources, negative sequence overcurrent (46) detects unbalanced faults. Set the overcurrent elements above maximum normal current with margin for measurement error and below the minimum fault current.

Coordinate with utility relays. The project's relays must trip faster than the utility's recloser on the feeder or the utility's zone 2 distance relay on the transmission line. Plot time-current curves for all relays in series and verify a minimum coordination interval (typically 0.3 seconds) between adjacent relay operating times at the maximum fault current.

Design anti-islanding protection per IEEE 1547-2018. Passive methods (voltage and frequency trip settings) detect most islanding conditions. For conditions where load and generation are closely matched, active methods (frequency shift, impedance measurement, or transfer trip from the utility breaker) are needed. Transfer trip via direct communication from the utility breaker to the project provides the most reliable detection.

Develop the trip logic. Define the sequence: fault detection, breaker trip, lockout, and reclosure blocking. For utility-side faults, the project must cease energization within 2 seconds (IEEE 1547 requirement). For project-side faults, coordinate with the utility to ensure the utility does not trip for faults that the project's relays will clear. Document all settings in a relay settings database for future coordination studies.

steps.description: Verify compliance with IEEE 1547-2018 and applicable grid code requirements through modeling, factory testing, and commissioning tests.

inputs.name: protection-scheme
inputs.desc: Relay settings and coordination study

inputs.name: anti-islanding-design
inputs.desc: Detection method and trip settings

outputs.name: compliance-verification-plan
outputs.desc: Test plan covering voltage ride-through, frequency ride-through, reactive power capability, ramp rate, and power quality

outputs.name: commissioning-test-results
outputs.desc: Measured performance against grid code requirements with pass/fail determination for each requirement

process: Define the compliance scope from IEEE 1547-2018 Category III (for projects above 500kVA on transmission): voltage ride-through (HVRT and LVRT curves), frequency ride-through, reactive power capability, voltage regulation mode, ramp rate limits, and power quality (harmonics per IEEE 519).

Verify voltage ride-through capability. The inverter must remain connected and inject reactive current during voltage sags per the Category III ride-through curve. Factory test certificates from the inverter manufacturer (per UL 1741 SB or IEC 62116) provide type-test evidence. Commissioning testing with controlled voltage injection confirms site-specific performance.

Verify reactive power capability. At rated active power, the inverter must deliver the specified reactive power range. Test at multiple active power levels (25%, 50%, 75%, 100%) and at both absorbing and injecting reactive power. Plot the measured P-Q capability curve against the requirement.

Verify power quality. Measure harmonic distortion at the POI during normal operation at various output levels. Total harmonic distortion must be below 5% for voltage and current, with individual harmonics below the limits in IEEE 519 Table 2 based on the short circuit ratio at the POI. Use a power quality analyzer with at least 50th harmonic measurement capability and 10-minute averaging per IEC 61000-4-7.

Document the commissioning test results in a report that includes: test equipment used with calibration certificates, test conditions (ambient temperature, irradiance for solar, wind speed for wind), measured values versus requirements, and a clear pass/fail determination for each grid code requirement. Submit to the utility for acceptance before commercial operation.

description: Engineer a wind energy project from resource assessment through rotor aerodynamics, structural loads, foundation design, and energy yield estimation.

steps.description: Characterize the wind resource at a site using measurement campaigns, statistical distribution fitting, and long-term correlation to produce a bankable energy estimate.

inputs.name: site-location
inputs.desc: Project site coordinates, terrain type, and land area

inputs.name: measurement-campaign-data
inputs.desc: Met mast or lidar data (minimum 12 months) with wind speed, direction, temperature, and pressure at multiple heights

outputs.name: wind-resource-characterization
outputs.desc: Long-term corrected wind speed distribution at hub height, wind rose, turbulence intensity, wind shear profile, and seasonal patterns

outputs.name: site-wind-parameters
outputs.desc: Weibull shape and scale parameters, IEC turbine class determination, and extreme wind speed estimates

process: Validate the measurement data. Check for sensor icing (flat-line periods in winter), tower shadow effects (speed deficit at azimuths behind the tower), and data recovery rate (require greater than 90% for bankability). Apply corrections for tower shadow using direction-dependent exclusion sectors.

Fit a Weibull distribution to the wind speed data at each measurement height. The two-parameter Weibull (shape k and scale A) is the industry standard. Method of moments or maximum likelihood estimation. Verify the fit with a chi-squared or Kolmogorov-Smirnov test. Typical onshore sites have k between 1.8 and 2.5.

Extrapolate to hub height using the wind shear profile. Measure shear from at least two heights on the met mast. The power law exponent alpha typically ranges from 0.10 (flat, smooth terrain) to 0.25 (rough, forested terrain). Use the log law with roughness length for more physics-based extrapolation. Lidar measurements above 100m reduce extrapolation uncertainty.

Correlate to long-term reference data. The measurement period (1-3 years) may not represent the long-term mean. Use MCP (Measure-Correlate-Predict) with a 10-20 year reference dataset (reanalysis data like ERA5, or a nearby long-term met station). Apply the correlation to adjust the on-site data to the long-term mean. This step typically shifts the annual mean wind speed by +/- 5% and is a major source of uncertainty.

Determine the IEC turbine class from the hub-height wind parameters. Class I: Vref = 50 m/s, Vave = 10 m/s. Class II: Vref = 42.5 m/s, Vave = 8.5 m/s. Class III: Vref = 37.5 m/s, Vave = 7.5 m/s. Turbulence category A (Iref = 0.16), B (0.14), or C (0.12). The turbine selected must be certified for a class equal to or above the site conditions.

steps.description: Design the wind turbine rotor using blade element momentum (BEM) theory: airfoil selection, blade chord and twist distribution, and performance optimization.

inputs.name: wind-resource-characterization
inputs.desc: Wind speed distribution and turbulence for performance optimization

inputs.name: site-wind-parameters
inputs.desc: IEC class and extreme wind for structural input

outputs.name: rotor-design
outputs.desc: Blade geometry (chord and twist vs span), airfoil distribution, design tip speed ratio, and rated/cut-in/cut-out wind speeds

outputs.name: power-curve
outputs.desc: Predicted power output vs wind speed from cut-in to cut-out, with Cp curve vs tip speed ratio

process: Select the design tip speed ratio (TSR). Optimal TSR for a three-bladed horizontal axis turbine is 6-8. Higher TSR means narrower chord (less material) but higher tip speeds (more noise and leading-edge erosion). The tip speed limit for onshore turbines is typically 80-85 m/s for noise compliance; offshore can go higher.

Apply BEM theory to determine the optimal chord and twist distribution. At each radial station, calculate the induction factors (axial a and tangential a-prime) that maximize the local power coefficient. The Glauert correction applies for high induction (a greater than 0.4). Prandtl's tip loss factor corrects for finite blade effects near the tip and root.

Select airfoils along the span. Thick airfoils (24-40% thickness) at the root for structural strength, transitioning to thin airfoils (15-21%) at the tip for aerodynamic efficiency. The DU and NACA 63-series are common. Roughness insensitivity matters for leading-edge contamination from insects and erosion. Flatback airfoils at the root improve Cl at high thickness ratios.

Optimize the blade for the annual energy production (AEP), not just peak Cp. The blade operates across a range of wind speeds with variable pitch and speed control. Below rated wind speed, the controller varies rotor speed to maintain optimal TSR. Above rated, pitch control limits power to rated. The optimization trades peak Cp against performance breadth across the wind speed distribution.

Generate the predicted power curve. At each wind speed, calculate the power from BEM including mechanical and electrical losses (gearbox if present, generator, converter, transformer). Apply air density corrections for the site altitude and temperature. The gap between the theoretical and measured power curve (typically 2-5%) accounts for yaw misalignment, turbulence effects, and control system imperfections.

steps.description: Calculate the structural loads on the wind turbine from design load cases per IEC 61400 and verify structural integrity of the tower, blades, and drivetrain.

inputs.name: rotor-design
inputs.desc: Blade geometry and aerodynamic properties

inputs.name: power-curve
inputs.desc: Operating parameters vs wind speed

outputs.name: design-load-envelope
outputs.desc: Ultimate and fatigue loads at key cross-sections (blade root, hub, tower top, tower base) from the governing DLCs

outputs.name: structural-verification
outputs.desc: Material utilization ratios for blades, tower, and foundation interface loads, with factors of safety

process: Define the design load cases (DLCs) per IEC 61400-1. The critical cases typically include: DLC 1.3 (power production with extreme turbulence), DLC 1.6 (power production with extreme coherent gust with direction change), DLC 2.3 (fault during operation with external grid loss), DLC 6.1 (parked, extreme wind with yaw misalignment), and DLC 1.2 (fatigue during normal power production).

Run aeroelastic simulations. Tools like OpenFAST, Bladed, or HAWC2 model the coupled aerodynamic, structural, and control system response. Each DLC requires multiple simulations with different turbulence seeds (6 seeds minimum per IEC 61400-1 for ultimate loads). Extract time series of forces and moments at key cross-sections.

Process ultimate loads. For each cross-section, identify the maximum and minimum values of each load component (Mx, My, Mz, Fx, Fy, Fz) across all DLC simulations. Apply the partial safety factor for loads (typically 1.35 for normal conditions). Compare against the cross-section capacity with a material partial safety factor (1.1-1.3 depending on material and failure mode).

Process fatigue loads. Extract load cycles using rainflow counting from the time series weighted by the annual wind speed distribution. Calculate the damage equivalent load (DEL) at each cross-section for a reference number of cycles (typically 1E7 for 20-year life). Compare the DEL against the material S-N curve (Goodman diagram for mean stress correction) to verify that the accumulated fatigue damage is less than 1.0.

Derive the foundation interface loads. The tower base loads (overturning moment, vertical force, horizontal shear, torsion) define the foundation design input. For onshore, the overturning moment at the tower base under DLC 6.1 (extreme wind, parked) typically governs the foundation size. Provide the full load envelope (ultimate and fatigue) to the foundation designer.

steps.description: Optimize the wind farm layout for energy production while managing wake losses, turbulence loading, and site constraints, then produce a bankable energy yield estimate.

inputs.name: design-load-envelope
inputs.desc: Structural limits that constrain minimum turbine spacing

inputs.name: structural-verification
inputs.desc: Verified turbine capability under site-specific loads

outputs.name: optimized-layout
outputs.desc: Turbine positions with wake loss analysis, turbulence intensity at each position, and noise contour map

outputs.name: energy-yield-estimate
outputs.desc: P50 and P90 annual energy production with uncertainty breakdown (resource, wake model, availability, electrical losses, curtailment)

process: Set spacing constraints. Minimum spacing of 3-4 rotor diameters crosswind and 7-10 rotor diameters downwind reduces wake losses to acceptable levels. Tighter spacing increases energy density (MW/km2) but increases wake losses and turbulence loading on downstream turbines. Site constraints (setbacks from property lines, roads, wetlands, residences) further limit positions.

Run wake modeling. The Jensen/Park model is the simplest (single-wake deficit proportional to thrust coefficient). The Fuga or Bastankhah models add turbulence and terrain effects. For complex terrain, CFD-based wake models improve accuracy but increase computation time. Array efficiency (ratio of actual production to sum of free-stream turbine production) for a well-designed onshore farm is typically 90-95%.

Optimize the layout using a genetic algorithm or particle swarm optimizer. The objective function is typically net AEP (including wake losses) or LCOE. Constraints include minimum spacing, setbacks, maximum turbulence intensity (must not exceed the turbine's IEC turbulence class), and noise limits at sensitive receptors.

Compile the energy yield estimate. Start with gross energy (each turbine's free-stream production from the power curve and wind resource). Subtract wake losses (from the wake model), availability losses (typically 2-5% for onshore, accounting for scheduled maintenance and unscheduled downtime), electrical losses (transformer and cable losses, typically 2-3%), environmental losses (icing, high-temperature shutdown, 0.5-2%), and curtailment (grid curtailment or noise curtailment, site-specific).

Quantify uncertainty for P90 estimation. Major uncertainty sources: long-term wind resource (3-5% sigma), wind speed measurement (1-2%), vertical extrapolation (1-3%), wake model (2-4%), power curve (2-3%), availability (1-2%). Combine in quadrature (RSS) for total uncertainty. P90 = P50 x (1 - 1.28 x sigma_total). A typical onshore project has P90/P50 ratio of 0.88-0.92.

description: Apply the fundamental methods of nuclear reactor design: neutronics, thermal-hydraulics, fuel design, reactivity control, and safety analysis.

steps.description: Apply neutron transport and diffusion theory to achieve criticality: four-factor formula, multiplication factor, and neutron economy optimization.

inputs.name: reactor-concept
inputs.desc: Reactor type (PWR, BWR, SMR, MSR, HTGR), thermal power rating, and target fuel cycle length

inputs.name: fuel-specification
inputs.desc: Fuel form (UO2, TRISO, metallic), enrichment target, and cladding material

outputs.name: neutronics-design
outputs.desc: Fuel assembly geometry, enrichment zoning, and beginning-of-life k-effective with margin for burnup reactivity swing

outputs.name: neutron-economy-analysis
outputs.desc: Four-factor formula breakdown (eta, f, p, epsilon), neutron leakage, and excess reactivity requiring control

process: Start with the four-factor formula: k_inf = eta x f x p x epsilon. Eta is the average number of fission neutrons per thermal neutron absorbed in fuel (about 2.06 for U-235 thermal fission). f is the thermal utilization factor (fraction of thermal absorptions in fuel vs total). p is the resonance escape probability (fraction of neutrons that slow down past U-238 resonances without capture). Epsilon is the fast fission factor (slight multiplication from fast fission in U-238, about 1.03).

Calculate k-effective by applying the non-leakage probability: k_eff = k_inf x P_NL, where P_NL depends on the geometric buckling B2 and the migration length M. For a cylindrical reactor, B2 = (2.405/R_extrapolated)2 + (pi/H_extrapolated)2. k_eff must equal 1.0 at steady state; the excess above 1.0 at beginning of life is managed by control systems.

Determine the excess reactivity needed. Over the fuel cycle, reactivity decreases as fissile material is consumed and fission products (especially Xe-135 and Sm-149) build up. The initial excess reactivity must compensate for this burnup swing (typically 10-20% delta_k/k for a PWR operating on an 18-month cycle). This excess is held down by control rods, soluble boron, and burnable absorbers.

Design the fuel assembly lattice. For a PWR, a 17x17 rod array is standard. The fuel rod pitch (center-to-center distance) determines the moderator-to-fuel ratio, which affects both f and p. Undermoderation (too tight a pitch) reduces f; overmoderation reduces p. The optimal ratio balances these for maximum k_inf. Enrichment zoning (lower enrichment at the periphery of the assembly) flattens the power distribution.

Run lattice physics calculations using a deterministic code (CASMO, HELIOS) or Monte Carlo (Serpent, OpenMC). Generate few-group cross sections as a function of burnup, moderator temperature, fuel temperature, and boron concentration. These feed into the core-level diffusion calculation for full-core power distribution, critical boron search, and shutdown margin verification.

steps.description: Design the fuel element: pellet geometry, cladding selection, gap conductance, fission gas management, and burnup limits.

inputs.name: neutronics-design
inputs.desc: Assembly geometry and enrichment for fuel rod specifications

inputs.name: neutron-economy-analysis
inputs.desc: Burnup target and power density for thermal limits

outputs.name: fuel-rod-design
outputs.desc: Pellet dimensions, cladding material and thickness, gap fill gas, plenum volume, and maximum burnup limit

outputs.name: fuel-performance-limits
outputs.desc: Maximum linear heat rate, centerline temperature limit, internal pressure limit, and cladding strain limit

process: Design the fuel pellet. UO2 pellets are typically 8-10mm diameter, 10-12mm height, with dished ends to accommodate axial thermal expansion and chamfered edges to ease loading. Theoretical density of UO2 is 10.97 g/cm3; pellets are sintered to 94-96% TD. Lower density provides porosity for fission gas storage but reduces uranium loading.

Select cladding material. Zircaloy-4 and M5 (Zr-Nb alloy) are standard for PWRs. Zirconium has a low thermal neutron absorption cross section (0.18 barns) and adequate corrosion resistance below 360C. Cladding thickness is 0.57-0.65mm, balancing neutron economy against burst and collapse strength. Advanced accident-tolerant fuels (Cr-coated Zr, FeCrAl, SiC/SiC) are entering qualification for enhanced high-temperature performance.

Design the pellet-cladding gap. Initial gap of 80-100 micrometers filled with helium (high thermal conductivity: 0.15 W/m-K at 300C). Gap conductance improves as burnup increases and the pellet swells into the cladding (pellet-cladding interaction). The gap conductance model (Ross-Stoute or equivalent) calculates the effective heat transfer coefficient across the gap as a function of gap width, gas composition, and contact pressure.

Size the fission gas plenum. Fission produces about 30 cm3 of gas (at STP) per MWd/kgU of burnup. At high burnup (50-60 MWd/kgU), fission gas release from the pellet matrix can reach 5-15% of total gas produced. The plenum volume (at the top of the fuel rod) must accommodate this gas without exceeding the internal pressure design limit (typically 15-17 MPa at end of life). Plenum-to-fuel volume ratio is typically 0.05-0.10.

Verify fuel performance limits. Maximum centerline temperature must stay below the UO2 melting point (2840C for fresh fuel, decreasing with burnup) with margin (limit typically set at 2590C). Maximum linear heat rate (power per unit length of fuel rod) is limited by centerline temperature, typically 40-44 kW/m for steady state. Cladding strain limit (1% plastic strain) prevents pellet-cladding mechanical interaction failures during power ramps.

steps.description: Design the reactor core thermal-hydraulics: coolant flow distribution, hot channel analysis, departure from nucleate boiling margin, and decay heat removal.

inputs.name: fuel-rod-design
inputs.desc: Rod geometry and maximum linear heat rate

inputs.name: fuel-performance-limits
inputs.desc: Temperature and strain limits for thermal margin calculation

outputs.name: thermal-hydraulic-design
outputs.desc: Core flow rate, inlet/outlet temperatures, pressure drop, and hot channel factors

outputs.name: dnb-margin-analysis
outputs.desc: Minimum DNBR and its location, with hot channel factor components (engineering, nuclear, flow)

process: Establish the core thermal parameters. For a PWR: inlet temperature around 290C, outlet temperature around 325C, system pressure 15.5 MPa, and coolant flow rate sized to achieve the target temperature rise across the core. Core delta-T = Qcore / (m_dot x Cp), where Qcore is total thermal power and Cp is the specific heat of water at operating conditions.

Calculate the hot channel factors. The nuclear hot channel factor F_q (ratio of peak to average linear heat rate) typically ranges from 2.0-2.5 including axial and radial peaking. The enthalpy rise hot channel factor F_delta_H (ratio of peak to average channel enthalpy rise) is typically 1.4-1.7. These are decomposed into nuclear factors (from the power distribution) and engineering factors (from manufacturing tolerances).

Perform the DNB analysis. Departure from nucleate boiling occurs when a vapor film blankets the fuel rod surface, causing a rapid temperature excursion. The DNBR (departure from nucleate boiling ratio) is the ratio of the predicted critical heat flux (from a CHF correlation like W-3 or WRB-2) to the actual local heat flux. Minimum DNBR must exceed the design limit (typically 1.30 for the W-3 correlation) at the most limiting location in the core.

Analyze the core pressure drop. Components: lower grid plate, fuel assembly inlet nozzle, spacer grids (8-10 per assembly), fuel rods (friction and form losses), upper nozzle, and upper grid plate. Total core delta-P is typically 150-200 kPa. The pressure drop distribution must ensure adequate flow to the hottest fuel assembly without flow instability.

Design the decay heat removal system. After shutdown, the fuel continues to generate heat from fission product decay: approximately 6% of full power at shutdown, decaying to 1.5% after one hour and 0.4% after one day. The residual heat removal system must remove this heat using redundant, safety-grade pumps and heat exchangers. The ultimate heat sink (river, cooling tower, or passive air) must be sized for decay heat removal under the most adverse environmental conditions.

steps.description: Design the reactivity control systems: control rods, soluble boron, and burnable absorbers, ensuring adequate shutdown margin and power distribution control.

inputs.name: thermal-hydraulic-design
inputs.desc: Core parameters that determine moderator temperature feedback

inputs.name: dnb-margin-analysis
inputs.desc: Power distribution limits that constrain control rod patterns

outputs.name: reactivity-control-design
outputs.desc: Control rod bank layout, boron letdown curve, and burnable absorber loading pattern

outputs.name: shutdown-margin-analysis
outputs.desc: Shutdown margin verification with the most reactive rod stuck out, including temperature defects and xenon effects

process: Design the control rod system. Rod cluster control assemblies (RCCAs) use 24 Ag-In-Cd or B4C absorber rodlets per cluster, inserted into guide tubes in the fuel assembly. Divide rods into shutdown banks (for reactor trip) and control banks (for power maneuvering). The worth of each bank depends on the neutron flux at the rod tip locations.

Size the soluble boron concentration. At beginning of cycle, soluble boron (boric acid in the coolant) holds down the excess reactivity that control rods cannot economically suppress. Typical BOC boron concentration is 1000-1600 ppm. The boron letdown curve (concentration vs burnup) tracks the reactivity decrease as fuel depletes. The moderator temperature coefficient must remain negative, which limits maximum boron concentration (boron makes the MTC less negative).

Design the burnable absorber loading. Integral fuel burnable absorbers (IFBA: ZrB2 coating on fuel pellets) or gadolinia (Gd2O3 mixed with UO2) deplete over the cycle, releasing reactivity to offset fuel depletion. This reduces the required soluble boron concentration (improving MTC) and flattens the radial power distribution. The absorber loading pattern is optimized cycle by cycle using a core design code.

Verify shutdown margin. With the reactor tripped and the most reactive control rod stuck fully withdrawn (single failure criterion), the core must remain subcritical by at least 1.3% delta_k/k. This must hold at the most reactive condition in the cycle, accounting for the moderator temperature defect (reactivity increase as coolant cools from operating to cold shutdown temperature) and xenon decay (reactivity increase as Xe-135 decays after shutdown).

Analyze power distribution control. Control rod insertion limits (rod insertion limits or RILs) prevent excessive axial peaking that could violate DNB limits. The operator maintains the axial offset (difference between top and bottom half power) within a target band using control bank stepping. Load-follow operations require coordinating rod movement, boron dilution/boration, and xenon transient management.

steps.description: Apply the safety analysis methodology for nuclear reactor licensing: design basis accidents, acceptance criteria, and defense in depth.

inputs.name: reactivity-control-design
inputs.desc: Control systems available for accident mitigation

inputs.name: shutdown-margin-analysis
inputs.desc: Shutdown capability under accident conditions

outputs.name: safety-analysis-results
outputs.desc: Results of the limiting design basis accidents showing compliance with acceptance criteria (peak cladding temperature, oxidation, coolable geometry)

outputs.name: defense-in-depth-assessment
outputs.desc: Evaluation of barrier integrity (fuel, cladding, primary boundary, containment) under normal, anticipated, and postulated accident conditions

process: Define the design basis events. These include anticipated operational occurrences (AOOs, frequency greater than 1E-2 per year: loss of feedwater, inadvertent rod withdrawal) and postulated accidents (frequency 1E-2 to 1E-6 per year: LOCA, steam line break, rod ejection). Each event is analyzed with conservative assumptions (single failure of active components, loss of offsite power coincident with the event).

Analyze the loss-of-coolant accident (LOCA). The large-break LOCA (guillotine rupture of the largest pipe) is analyzed in three phases: blowdown (rapid depressurization), refill (ECCS injection refills the lower plenum), and reflood (core is recovered). Acceptance criteria per 10 CFR 50.46: peak cladding temperature less than 2200F (1204C), local oxidation less than 17% of cladding thickness, hydrogen generation less than 1% of total zirconium, coolable geometry maintained, and long-term cooling assured.

Analyze the reactivity insertion accident (RIA). The limiting event is a control rod ejection due to a failure of the control rod drive mechanism housing. The energy deposited in the fuel must remain below 280 cal/g to prevent fuel dispersal. The analysis uses point kinetics with Doppler feedback (the fuel temperature coefficient provides inherent negative feedback that limits the power excursion).

Analyze the anticipated transient without scram (ATWS). Per 10 CFR 50.62, the plant must be able to maintain an acceptable condition if the reactor protection system fails to trip the reactor during an anticipated transient. This requires a diverse scram system (AMSAC for PWRs) and demonstrates that peak RCS pressure remains below the ASME Service Level C limit.

Assess defense in depth. The five levels: Level 1 (prevention of abnormal conditions through conservative design and quality), Level 2 (detection and control of abnormal conditions through reactor protection and control systems), Level 3 (control of design basis accidents through engineered safety features), Level 4 (mitigation of severe accidents through containment and emergency procedures), Level 5 (emergency response through offsite emergency planning). Document how each barrier (fuel matrix, cladding, reactor coolant boundary, containment) is protected at each level.

description: Design a hydrogen production system from electrolyzer selection through balance of plant, efficiency analysis, cost modeling, and safety engineering.

steps.description: Select the electrolysis technology by matching application requirements to the operating characteristics, efficiency, and maturity of PEM, alkaline, and solid oxide electrolyzers.

inputs.name: production-target
inputs.desc: Required hydrogen output in kg/day or Nm3/hr, purity specification, and delivery pressure

inputs.name: power-source-profile
inputs.desc: Electricity source (grid, solar, wind, hybrid), variability profile, availability factor, and cost per MWh

outputs.name: electrolyzer-selection
outputs.desc: Selected technology with rated capacity, stack efficiency curve, turndown ratio, ramp rate, and expected stack lifetime

outputs.name: technology-comparison
outputs.desc: Side-by-side comparison of PEM, alkaline, and SOEC on efficiency, cost, durability, dynamic response, and technology readiness

process: Characterize the duty cycle. If the power source is variable (solar or wind), the electrolyzer must handle frequent load changes. PEM electrolyzers respond in seconds and tolerate 5-100% load range. Alkaline electrolyzers are slower (minutes for large load steps) with a typical minimum load of 20-40%. SOEC operates at high temperature (700-850C) and is best suited for steady-state baseload operation where waste heat is available.

Compare stack efficiency. The thermodynamic minimum for water splitting is 39.4 kWh per kg H2 (higher heating value basis). PEM stacks operate at 50-65 kWh/kg at rated power. Alkaline stacks achieve 50-60 kWh/kg. SOEC achieves 35-45 kWh/kg by substituting heat for electricity (Faradaic efficiency above 95% at operating temperature). Express efficiency as kWh per kg H2 or as a percentage of HHV (HHV of H2 = 39.4 kWh/kg).

Evaluate capital cost and stack lifetime. PEM: higher capital cost (800-1500 $/kW) but improving rapidly; stack lifetime 60,000-80,000 hours. Alkaline: lower capital cost (500-1000 $/kW), more mature supply chain; stack lifetime 80,000-100,000 hours. SOEC: highest capital cost currently (1500-3000 $/kW), limited commercial deployment; stack degradation is the main challenge (1-3% per 1000 hours).

Assess water quality requirements. PEM requires deionized water (less than 1 microsiemens/cm conductivity) to protect the proton exchange membrane. Alkaline uses a KOH electrolyte (25-30% concentration) and is less sensitive to water purity. SOEC uses steam, which must be clean but not ultrapure. Water consumption is approximately 9 liters per kg H2 produced.

Select based on the application fit. For renewable-coupled (variable power): PEM for its dynamic response, unless budget constraints favor alkaline with an intermediate buffer. For industrial baseload with available heat: SOEC for its superior electrical efficiency. For cost-sensitive, steady-state grid-connected: alkaline for its lower capital cost and proven durability.

steps.description: Design the balance of plant: power conditioning, water treatment, gas processing, compression, storage, and control systems.

inputs.name: electrolyzer-selection
inputs.desc: Technology, rated capacity, and operating parameters

inputs.name: technology-comparison
inputs.desc: Technology-specific BOP requirements

outputs.name: bop-design
outputs.desc: Power supply sizing, water treatment train, gas dryer and purifier, compressor selection, and storage vessel sizing

outputs.name: process-flow-diagram
outputs.desc: Complete PFD with mass and energy balance at rated and partial load conditions

process: Design the power supply. For grid-connected: AC/DC rectifier (thyristor or IGBT-based) sized for stack voltage range and current. For renewable-coupled: DC/DC converter or direct connection (for PV) with MPPT. The power electronics must handle the stack's voltage-current characteristic: voltage increases with current (the polarization curve) and changes with temperature and degradation.

Design the water treatment system. Raw water passes through multimedia filtration, activated carbon, reverse osmosis (to less than 10 microsiemens/cm), and electrodeionization or mixed-bed ion exchange (to less than 1 microsiemens/cm for PEM). Size for peak water consumption plus 30% for RO reject and system flushing. Include a water storage tank for at least 4 hours of production.

Design the gas processing system. Hydrogen from the electrolyzer is saturated with water vapor. A condenser and desiccant dryer reduce moisture to the delivery specification (typically less than 5 ppm for fuel cell grade, ISO 14687). For PEM, oxygen crossover produces trace oxygen in the hydrogen stream; a deoxo reactor (catalytic recombiner) reduces O2 to less than 1 ppm if required.

Select the compressor. Electrolyzer output pressure is 1-30 bar depending on technology. If delivery or storage pressure is higher (350-700 bar for vehicle refueling, 200-350 bar for tube trailer), a multi-stage diaphragm or ionic liquid compressor is needed. Size for rated flow with a capacity margin. Compression energy is significant: approximately 2-4 kWh/kg H2 for compression from 30 to 350 bar.

Size the storage. Buffer storage between the electrolyzer and the offtaker smooths production-demand mismatch. For ground-level storage, Type I (steel) or Type II (steel liner with composite wrap) vessels at 200-500 bar. Size the storage volume from the maximum expected production-demand mismatch duration. For large volumes, geological storage (salt caverns) offers the lowest cost per kg stored.

steps.description: Build the efficiency chain and cost model: LCOH calculation, sensitivity to electricity price, and comparison against incumbent hydrogen production methods.

inputs.name: bop-design
inputs.desc: BOP equipment sizing and energy consumption

inputs.name: process-flow-diagram
inputs.desc: Mass and energy balance for efficiency calculation

outputs.name: efficiency-chain
outputs.desc: Electrical-to-hydrogen efficiency at rated and partial load, including all parasitic loads (BOP, compression, cooling)

outputs.name: lcoh-analysis
outputs.desc: Levelized cost of hydrogen in $/kg with breakdown by electricity, capex, stack replacement, and O&M, plus sensitivity to key variables

process: Calculate the overall system efficiency. Start with stack efficiency (kWh_DC / kg_H2), add rectifier losses (2-4%), BOP parasitics (pumps, fans, controls: 3-8% of rated power), compression energy, and cooling energy. The total specific energy consumption for a PEM system is typically 55-70 kWh/kg H2 including all parasitics. Express as a percentage of HHV: system efficiency = 39.4 / total_kWh_per_kg x 100%.

Build the LCOH model. LCOH = (Annualized_Capex + Annual_Opex + Annual_Stack_Replacement_Cost + Annual_Electricity_Cost) / Annual_H2_Production. Annualized capex uses CRF (capital recovery factor) from discount rate and project life. Stack replacement is a periodic cost (every 7-10 years for PEM, 10-12 years for alkaline) discounted to present value.

Electricity cost dominates LCOH. At 50 $/MWh and 55 kWh/kg, electricity alone is 2.75 $/kg H2. At 20 $/MWh (low-cost renewables), it drops to 1.10 $/kg. Capex contribution at current PEM costs (1000 $/kW, 4000 full-load hours) is approximately 1.50-2.00 $/kg. O&M adds 0.20-0.50 $/kg. Total LCOH for green hydrogen today is typically 3-6 $/kg depending on electricity cost and utilization.

Run sensitivity analysis. The variables with the largest impact: electricity price (+/- 10 $/MWh), capacity factor (+/- 1000 hours), stack efficiency degradation rate (+/- 0.5%/year), capex (+/- 30%), and stack replacement cost (+/- 50%). Present as a tornado chart. The breakeven electricity price against grey hydrogen (SMR at 1.50-2.00 $/kg with no carbon price) is approximately 15-25 $/MWh.

Evaluate the round-trip efficiency for power-to-gas-to-power (P2G2P). Electrolysis at 65% efficiency, compression at 90%, storage losses negligible for short-term, fuel cell or turbine at 40-60% efficiency. Total round-trip: 23-35%. This makes hydrogen energy storage expensive compared to batteries for short duration but competitive for seasonal storage where the alternative is curtailment.

steps.description: Apply hydrogen safety engineering: hazard identification, ATEX zone classification, ventilation design, detection systems, and emergency response planning.

inputs.name: efficiency-chain
inputs.desc: Operating parameters that define the safety envelope

inputs.name: lcoh-analysis
inputs.desc: System configuration for hazard analysis scope

outputs.name: safety-design
outputs.desc: ATEX zone classifications, ventilation rates, detection system specification, and passive safety features

outputs.name: emergency-response-plan
outputs.desc: Leak scenarios, escalation criteria, automatic shutdowns, and emergency procedures

process: Characterize hydrogen hazards. Hydrogen is flammable in air from 4% to 75% by volume (the widest flammable range of any common fuel). Minimum ignition energy is 0.02 mJ (one-tenth of natural gas). Flame speed is high (3.5 m/s laminar) and detonation is possible in confined spaces above 18% concentration. Hydrogen flames are nearly invisible in daylight. Hydrogen embrittlement affects carbon steel above a threshold pressure (dependent on steel grade and temperature).

Classify ATEX zones per IEC 60079-10-1. Zone 0: inside the electrolyzer stack and gas processing equipment (continuous explosive atmosphere). Zone 1: within 1 meter of potential release points (flanges, valves, fittings) where occasional leaks are expected. Zone 2: further afield where explosive atmosphere is not expected but possible under abnormal conditions. Equipment in each zone must be certified to the corresponding equipment category.

Design ventilation. For indoor installations, mechanical ventilation must prevent hydrogen accumulation above 25% of the lower flammability limit (1% H2 by volume) under the maximum credible leak rate. The required air flow rate follows from the leak rate and the dilution factor: V_dot = Q_leak / (0.01 x safety_factor), where safety_factor is typically 4. For outdoor installations, natural ventilation often suffices if equipment spacing meets the minimum separation distances.

Specify detection systems. Install hydrogen detectors at the ceiling (hydrogen rises at 20 m/s in still air), near potential leak sources, and in enclosed or semi-enclosed areas. Catalytic bead sensors for general area monitoring (range 0-100% LEL, response time less than 30 seconds). Set alarm at 20% LEL (0.8% H2) for warning and 40% LEL (1.6% H2) for automatic shutdown and ventilation increase. Cross-sensitivity to other gases must be characterized.

Design the emergency shutdown system. Automatic triggers: hydrogen detection above 40% LEL, fire detection, loss of ventilation, seismic event above threshold, or manual emergency stop. Shutdown sequence: close hydrogen supply valves (fail-closed), de-energize the electrolyzer stack, purge hydrogen lines with nitrogen, and activate enhanced ventilation. The shutdown must complete within 60 seconds of the trigger. Document the emergency response procedures including evacuation zones (minimum 15-meter radius for outdoor releases) and coordination with local emergency services.

description: Design power electronic converters for renewable energy applications: inverter topology, grid-forming control, MPPT, filter design, and thermal management.

steps.description: Select the inverter topology for grid-tied renewable applications based on power level, voltage, efficiency, and harmonic performance requirements.

inputs.name: system-requirements
inputs.desc: Power rating, DC input voltage range, AC grid voltage, efficiency target, and harmonic limits

inputs.name: application-context
inputs.desc: Solar/wind/battery, utility-scale or distributed, outdoor or indoor installation

outputs.name: topology-selection
outputs.desc: Selected topology with switching device ratings, number of levels, modulation strategy, and predicted efficiency curve

outputs.name: topology-trade-off-analysis
outputs.desc: Comparison of candidate topologies on efficiency, cost, complexity, harmonic performance, and common-mode voltage

process: Map the application to a topology class. Two-level voltage source inverter (VSI): simplest, lowest cost, adequate for string inverters up to 100kW. Three-level NPC (neutral point clamped): halves the device voltage stress and reduces output harmonics, standard for central inverters 500kW-4MW. T-type (three-level active NPC): combines advantages of two-level (fewer devices at zero crossing) and NPC (reduced dv/dt), suitable for 100-500kW. Modular multilevel converter (MMC): for HVDC and very high power.

Select switching devices. For 1500V DC systems: 1200V SiC MOSFETs or 1700V Si IGBTs in a two-level topology, or 900-1200V devices in a three-level. SiC offers lower switching losses (enabling higher switching frequency or higher efficiency) at higher cost per amp. Si IGBTs are cost-effective above 100kW and available in high-current modules. GaN is entering the market for lower-power string inverters.

Choose the modulation strategy. Space vector PWM (SVPWM) maximizes DC bus utilization (15% higher than sinusoidal PWM) and provides lower harmonic distortion. For three-level topologies, SVPWM with neutral point balancing prevents DC bus capacitor voltage drift. Discontinuous PWM reduces switching losses by clamping one phase to the rail for a portion of each cycle, trading harmonic performance for efficiency at partial load.

Predict the efficiency curve. Calculate losses at each operating point: conduction losses (from device I-V characteristics and current waveform), switching losses (from switching energy curves and switching frequency), and gate driver losses. For SiC at 16kHz switching frequency, typical inverter efficiency is 98.5-99% at rated power. Partial-load efficiency matters for solar (CEC-weighted efficiency emphasizes 10-75% loading).

Evaluate common-mode voltage. Two-level inverters generate high-frequency common-mode voltage steps equal to Vdc/2, causing leakage current through parasitic capacitances to ground. This is a concern for transformerless solar inverters (leakage current through PV module frame capacitance). Three-level topologies reduce common-mode steps to Vdc/4. H5, H6, and HERIC topologies specifically address common-mode voltage in single-phase transformerless applications.

steps.description: Design the inverter control system: grid-following for stable grids, grid-forming for weak grids and microgrids, with voltage and frequency regulation.

inputs.name: topology-selection
inputs.desc: Inverter topology and switching characteristics

inputs.name: topology-trade-off-analysis
inputs.desc: Harmonic and dynamic performance characteristics

outputs.name: control-architecture
outputs.desc: Grid-following or grid-forming control structure with tuned controller parameters

outputs.name: stability-analysis
outputs.desc: Small-signal stability analysis showing gain and phase margins, and impedance-based stability assessment for weak grid conditions

process: Choose between grid-following and grid-forming. Grid-following inverters use a phase-locked loop (PLL) to synchronize with the grid voltage and inject current at the grid frequency. They require a stiff voltage reference and become unstable when the short circuit ratio (SCR) at the POI drops below 2-3. Grid-forming inverters create their own voltage reference and frequency, behaving like a voltage source behind an impedance. They can operate in weak grids (SCR less than 2) and in island mode.

Design the grid-following controller. Inner current loop: PI controller in the dq synchronous reference frame, bandwidth 500-2000 Hz (one-tenth to one-fifth of switching frequency). Feed-forward of grid voltage decouples the d and q axes. Outer power loop: PI controller generating current references from active and reactive power setpoints, bandwidth 5-50 Hz. PLL bandwidth 10-50 Hz; lower bandwidth improves stability in weak grids but slows transient response.

Design the grid-forming controller. Virtual synchronous machine (VSM) emulates a synchronous generator: the swing equation provides frequency regulation (virtual inertia H = 2-10 seconds), and a reactive power droop provides voltage regulation. Alternative: droop control (P-f and Q-V droop) is simpler but provides no inertial response. The output impedance of the grid-forming inverter must be predominantly inductive for stable power sharing.

Perform stability analysis. Small-signal model: linearize the inverter, filter, and grid model around the operating point. Calculate eigenvalues and participation factors to identify potential oscillatory modes. Impedance-based analysis: measure or model the inverter output impedance Zs and the grid impedance Zg. The system is stable if the ratio Zs/Zg satisfies the Nyquist criterion (no encirclement of -1). Weak grids increase the magnitude of Zg, potentially causing instability.

Implement grid-support functions. Frequency response: reduce power output when frequency exceeds 60.05 Hz (overfrequency droop), increase power (if available) when frequency drops below 59.95 Hz. Voltage regulation: adjust reactive power output to maintain POI voltage within the dead band. Fault ride-through: inject reactive current proportional to voltage depression during grid faults (typically 2% additional reactive current per 1% voltage drop, up to rated current).

steps.description: Design the LCL output filter for grid-connected inverters to meet harmonic injection limits while minimizing losses, size, and cost.

inputs.name: control-architecture
inputs.desc: Control bandwidth and modulation strategy affecting harmonic spectrum

inputs.name: stability-analysis
inputs.desc: Impedance characteristics affecting filter resonance damping

outputs.name: filter-design
outputs.desc: LCL filter component values (inductors and capacitors), damping method, and predicted harmonic spectrum at the POI

outputs.name: filter-loss-analysis
outputs.desc: Copper and core losses in filter inductors, capacitor ESR losses, and total filter efficiency impact

process: Set the design targets. The LCL filter must attenuate switching-frequency harmonics to meet IEEE 519 limits at the POI: individual harmonics below the limits in Table 2 (dependent on ISC/IL ratio), total demand distortion (TDD) below 5% for typical utility-scale. The filter resonant frequency must be between 10x the fundamental (600 Hz for 60 Hz systems) and 0.5x the switching frequency to avoid exciting resonance with either the control bandwidth or the switching harmonics.

Size the inverter-side inductor L1. L1 limits the peak-to-peak current ripple at the switching frequency. Target ripple of 10-25% of rated peak current. L1 = Vdc / (8 x fsw x delta_I_pp) for a two-level inverter with SVPWM. For a three-level inverter, the effective switching frequency seen by L1 doubles, so L1 can be halved for the same ripple. L1 inductance is typically 5-15% of base impedance.

Size the filter capacitor Cf. The capacitor provides a low-impedance path for switching-frequency current, shunting it away from the grid. Limit reactive power absorbed by Cf to less than 5% of rated power: Cf less than 0.05 x Prated / (omega x Vline2). Typical values: 1-5% of base impedance. Larger Cf improves filtering but increases reactive current and may cause leading power factor at light load.

Size the grid-side inductor L2. The resonant frequency of the LCL filter is f_res = 1/(2pi) x sqrt((L1+L2)/(L1 x L2 x Cf)). Choose L2 to place the resonant frequency in the target range. L2 is typically 0.5-2x L1. Verify that the total inductance (L1 + L2) does not exceed the maximum that allows the inverter to deliver rated current at the minimum DC bus voltage.

Design the damping. Passive damping: a resistor in series with Cf dissipates resonant energy but adds losses (typically 0.5-1% of rated power). Active damping: the inverter control loop adds virtual resistance at the resonant frequency (capacitor current feedback or notch filter). Active damping eliminates the power loss but requires accurate resonant frequency knowledge and adequate control bandwidth. For utility-scale inverters, active damping is standard; passive damping is a fallback for simpler control systems.

steps.description: Design the thermal management for power electronic converters in outdoor renewable energy enclosures: loss modeling, heat sink sizing, and reliability prediction.

inputs.name: filter-design
inputs.desc: Filter losses that add to the thermal load

inputs.name: filter-loss-analysis
inputs.desc: Quantified losses in filter components

outputs.name: thermal-design
outputs.desc: Heat sink selection, cooling method, enclosure rating, and junction temperature prediction across the operating range

outputs.name: reliability-estimate
outputs.desc: Expected component life based on thermal cycling and steady-state junction temperature

process: Calculate the total thermal load.
