Sum the losses from all heat-generating components: switching devices (conduction + switching losses from the topology analysis), filter inductors (copper + core losses), filter capacitors (ESR losses), gate drivers, control electronics, and auxiliary power supplies. At rated power, total losses for a 98.5% efficient inverter at 1 MW are approximately 15 kW.

Design the semiconductor thermal path. The thermal resistance from junction to ambient is the series sum: Rth_j-c (junction to case, from datasheet) + Rth_c-s (case to heat sink, from thermal interface material) + Rth_s-a (heat sink to ambient, from the heat sink design). Calculate the required Rth_s-a from: Tj_max = Tamb_max + Ptotal x (Rth_j-c + Rth_c-s + Rth_s-a). For IGBT modules, Tj_max is typically 150C; for SiC MOSFETs, 175C.

Select the cooling method. For inverters up to 100kW, forced-air cooling with aluminum extrusion heat sinks is typical. For 100kW-4MW, liquid cooling (glycol-water through cold plates) provides lower thermal resistance and more compact design. Size the liquid cooling loop: flow rate from Q = m_dot x Cp x delta_T, where delta_T is the allowable coolant temperature rise (typically 10-15C). Include a radiator or heat exchanger to reject heat to ambient.

Design for the outdoor environment. Inverter enclosures for outdoor installation are typically IP65 (dust-tight, water-jet protected). The enclosure adds thermal resistance between the internal air and ambient. Internal fans circulate air across heat-generating components, while external fans or liquid-to-air heat exchangers reject heat. Derate the inverter output at high ambient temperatures: above the rated ambient (typically 45-50C), reduce power output linearly to maintain junction temperature below the limit.

Predict reliability from thermal cycling. Power semiconductor lifetime is limited by bond wire fatigue and solder fatigue from thermal cycling. The Coffin-Manson model predicts cycles to failure from the temperature swing delta_Tj and the mean temperature Tj_mean: Nf = A x delta_Tj^(-alpha) x exp(Ea/(k x Tj_mean)), where alpha is typically 4-6 for bond wire fatigue. For a solar inverter with daily thermal cycles of 40-60C swing, expected power module lifetime is 15-25 years. Design for module replacement as a maintenance item.

description: Design the electrical protection system for power networks: fault analysis, relay coordination, differential protection, arc flash assessment, and microgrid protection.

steps.description: Calculate fault currents using symmetrical components: positive, negative, and zero sequence networks for three-phase, line-to-line, line-to-ground, and double-line-to-ground faults.

inputs.name: system-one-line-diagram
inputs.desc: Network topology with equipment ratings, impedances, and transformer connections

inputs.name: equipment-data
inputs.desc: Generator subtransient reactances, transformer impedances, cable and line impedances, and source short circuit capacity

outputs.name: fault-current-results
outputs.desc: Three-phase, SLG, LL, and DLG fault currents at each bus, with symmetrical and asymmetrical (DC offset) values

outputs.name: sequence-impedance-model
outputs.desc: Positive, negative, and zero sequence impedance matrices for the network

process: Build the sequence networks. The positive sequence network is the normal power flow network with all sources and impedances. The negative sequence network has the same topology but generators are represented by their negative sequence reactance (approximately equal to subtransient reactance for round-rotor machines). The zero sequence network depends on transformer winding connections: delta windings block zero sequence current; wye-grounded windings pass it.

Calculate the three-phase fault current. This uses only the positive sequence network: I_fault_3ph = V_prefault / Z1_total, where Z1_total is the positive sequence impedance from the source to the fault point. This is the simplest and often the highest-magnitude fault.

Calculate the single-line-to-ground (SLG) fault current. Connect the three sequence networks in series at the fault point: I_fault_SLG = 3 x V_prefault / (Z1 + Z2 + Z0 + 3Zf), where Zf is the fault impedance. In solidly-grounded systems, the SLG fault current can exceed the three-phase fault current when Z0 is less than Z1.

Apply the DC offset for asymmetrical fault current. The first half-cycle peak is the RMS symmetrical current times the asymmetry factor: I_peak = I_rms_sym x sqrt(2) x (1 + e^(-t/(X/R x T))), where X/R is the system X/R ratio at the fault point and T is the half-cycle period. The momentary (first cycle) and interrupting (3-5 cycle) duty factors from IEEE C37 standards convert symmetrical RMS to the values used for equipment rating verification.

Verify equipment ratings. Compare the calculated fault currents against the interrupting rating of circuit breakers, the withstand rating of buses and cables, and the through-fault capability of transformers. If the available fault current exceeds the equipment rating, either upgrade the equipment or install current-limiting devices (fuses, current-limiting reactors, or is-limiters).

steps.description: Coordinate protective relays through the power system: overcurrent, distance, and directional elements, ensuring selectivity, sensitivity, and speed.

inputs.name: fault-current-results
inputs.desc: Fault currents at each bus for relay setting calculations

inputs.name: sequence-impedance-model
inputs.desc: Network impedances for distance relay reach calculations

outputs.name: relay-settings
outputs.desc: Pickup values, time dials, instantaneous settings, and coordination time intervals for each relay

outputs.name: coordination-study
outputs.desc: Time-current curves plotted for each protection zone showing coordination between primary and backup relays

process: Define the protection zones. Each zone has a primary relay (fast clearing) and at least one backup relay (clears if the primary fails, after a time delay). Zones overlap: the downstream relay's instantaneous zone should not reach into the upstream relay's zone. Work from the load toward the source when setting overcurrent relays.

Set the overcurrent relay pickup (50/51). The time-overcurrent (51) pickup must be above maximum load current with margin (typically 1.25-1.5x) and below minimum fault current in the protected zone. Select the time-current curve (inverse, very inverse, extremely inverse) based on the downstream device characteristics: extremely inverse curves coordinate well with fuse curves; inverse curves suit motor starting and transformer inrush.

Set the time dial for coordination. At the maximum fault current seen by both the upstream and downstream relays, the upstream relay must clear at least 0.3-0.4 seconds after the downstream relay (the coordination time interval, CTI). This accounts for relay operating time tolerance, circuit breaker clearing time, and relay overtravel. Work upstream from the most remote device, adding the CTI at each level.

Set instantaneous (50) elements. The instantaneous pickup is set above the maximum fault current that the downstream relay should clear (typically 125% of the maximum through-fault current for the next downstream bus). This provides fast clearing for faults close to the relay location without waiting for the time-overcurrent curve.

Verify coordination graphically. Plot all relay time-current curves, fuse curves, transformer damage curves, and cable damage curves on the same log-log axes. Verify: no overlap between adjacent relay curves at any fault current level (selectivity), all relays can detect the minimum fault current in their zone (sensitivity), and all faults are cleared within the equipment damage time (speed). Document the settings in a relay database for future maintenance and re-coordination.

steps.description: Perform arc flash analysis per IEEE 1584 to determine incident energy, arc flash boundaries, and required PPE at each working location in the power system.

inputs.name: relay-settings
inputs.desc: Protection device clearing times that determine arc duration

inputs.name: coordination-study
inputs.desc: Fault clearing sequence for arc duration calculation at each bus

outputs.name: arc-flash-results
outputs.desc: Incident energy in cal/cm2 at each bus, arc flash boundary distance, and required PPE category

outputs.name: arc-flash-labels
outputs.desc: Equipment labels per NFPA 70E with incident energy, boundary, PPE requirement, and working distance

process: Determine the arcing current. IEEE 1584-2018 provides empirical equations for arcing current as a function of bolted fault current, system voltage, electrode gap, electrode configuration (VCB, VCBB, HCB, VOA, HOA), and enclosure size. The arcing current is less than the bolted fault current because the arc impedance limits current. Calculate arcing current for both the maximum and reduced (85%) bolted fault current to capture the worst case (reduced arcing current may result in longer clearing time and higher incident energy).

Determine the arc duration. The arc duration is the time from arc initiation to the upstream protective device clearing the fault. Read the clearing time from the relay or fuse time-current curve at the arcing current (not the bolted fault current). For current-limiting fuses, the clearing time is less than one half-cycle for currents above the fuse's current-limiting threshold.

Calculate incident energy. IEEE 1584-2018: E = Cf x En x (t/0.2) x (610^x / D^x), where the intermediate variables come from the electrode configuration model. The working distance D is the distance from the arc source to the worker's face and chest (typically 455mm for low-voltage switchgear, 910mm for medium-voltage). Express results in cal/cm2.

Determine the arc flash boundary. The arc flash boundary is the distance at which incident energy equals the onset of second-degree burn (1.2 cal/cm2). Solve the incident energy equation for distance D where E = 1.2. This boundary defines the restricted approach zone where PPE is required.

Assign PPE categories per NFPA 70E Table 130.7(C)(15)(c). Category 1: 4 cal/cm2 (arc-rated shirt and pants, safety glasses). Category 2: 8 cal/cm2 (arc-rated shirt, pants, face shield, hard hat). Category 3: 25 cal/cm2 (arc flash suit with hood). Category 4: 40 cal/cm2 (multi-layer arc flash suit). Above 40 cal/cm2, work is not permitted until the hazard is reduced (de-energize, add faster protection, or install arc-resistant switchgear). Generate equipment labels with all required information.

description: Apply high-voltage engineering methods: insulation coordination, cable design, surge protection, transformer condition assessment, and substation design.

steps.description: Design the insulation coordination for a high-voltage system: select BIL and BSL ratings, determine clearances, and specify surge protection to protect equipment from lightning and switching surges.

inputs.name: system-voltage-class
inputs.desc: Nominal system voltage, maximum operating voltage, and isokeraunic level of the area

inputs.name: equipment-catalog
inputs.desc: Available BIL ratings for transformers, bushings, CTs, PTs, and circuit breakers in the voltage class

outputs.name: insulation-levels
outputs.desc: Selected BIL and BSL for each piece of equipment, with coordination margins to surge arrester protective levels

outputs.name: clearance-requirements
outputs.desc: Phase-to-ground and phase-to-phase clearances per IEEE C2 (NESC) and IEC 60071

process: Determine the standard insulation level (BIL) for the system voltage class. IEEE C57.12.00 and IEC 60071-1 provide standard BIL values. For 138kV systems: standard BIL is 550 or 650kV. For 230kV: 900 or 1050kV. For 345kV: 1050 or 1300kV. Higher BIL provides more margin but costs more (larger bushings, greater clearances, more insulating material in transformers).

Select and apply surge arresters. Metal oxide (ZnO) surge arresters limit transient overvoltages to their protective level. Select the arrester MCOV (maximum continuous operating voltage) above the maximum line-to-ground operating voltage. The arrester protective level (at the switching surge and lightning impulse current levels) must be below the equipment BIL with a protection margin of at least 15-20% for lightning and 15% for switching surges.

Calculate the protective margin. PM = (BIL_equipment - V_protective_level_arrester) / V_protective_level_arrester x 100%. If the margin is less than the minimum, either increase the equipment BIL or select a lower-protective-level arrester (lower MCOV). For transformer protection, the arrester must be mounted as close as possible to the transformer terminals; each meter of lead wire adds approximately 1kV to the effective protective level during fast-front transients.

Determine clearances. Phase-to-ground clearance depends on the BIL and the altitude (clearances increase above 1000m due to reduced air density). IEEE C2 (NESC) Table 124-1 provides minimum clearances for various BIL levels. Phase-to-phase clearance is typically 1.05-1.15 times the phase-to-ground clearance. Working clearances for personnel must meet NESC Rule 124 or OSHA 1910.269 minimum approach distances.

Address switching surge insulation coordination for systems 345kV and above. Switching surges (from breaker operations, line energization, fault clearing) produce overvoltages of 1.5-3.0 per unit. Pre-insertion resistors or controlled switching (synchronized breaker closing near voltage zero) limit switching surges to 1.5-2.0 per unit. The BSL (basic switching surge insulation level) must exceed the maximum switching surge with margin. Arresters also limit switching surges but must be rated for the associated energy duty.

steps.description: Design high-voltage cables: insulation selection, conductor sizing for ampacity, thermal analysis, and installation method considerations.

inputs.name: insulation-levels
inputs.desc: Required insulation level for cable voltage rating

inputs.name: clearance-requirements
inputs.desc: Installation constraints from clearance and separation requirements

outputs.name: cable-specification
outputs.desc: Cable type, conductor size, insulation material and thickness, shield design, and jacket material

outputs.name: ampacity-calculation
outputs.desc: Continuous ampacity for the installation conditions, with derating factors for ambient temperature, soil thermal resistivity, depth of burial, and mutual heating

process: Select the cable insulation. XLPE (cross-linked polyethylene) is standard for new installations at 69-500kV: low dielectric losses, no oil maintenance, 90C continuous conductor temperature rating. EPR (ethylene propylene rubber) offers better flexibility for difficult routing but higher dielectric losses. Fluid-filled cables (HPFF, SCFF) remain in service but are rarely specified for new installations due to environmental concerns. For submarine cables, XLPE with lead sheath and wire armor is standard.

Size the conductor. Start with the required ampacity (current from the power flow study, including emergency and future load growth). The conductor cross section determines the DC resistance. Apply the AC resistance factor (skin effect and proximity effect) which increases resistance by 5-20% above DC resistance for large conductors at 60Hz. Common conductor materials: copper for minimum size, aluminum for minimum weight and cost.

Calculate the ampacity using IEC 60287 or Neher-McGrath method. The cable temperature rise above ambient is: delta_T = (Wc + 0.5 x Wd) x T1 + (Wc + Wd + Ws) x n x T2 + (Wc + Wd + Ws) x n x T3, where Wc = conductor losses, Wd = dielectric losses, Ws = shield losses, T1 = thermal resistance of insulation, T2 = thermal resistance of jacket and bedding, T3 = thermal resistance of surrounding medium. Solve for the current that makes the conductor temperature equal to 90C.

Apply derating factors. Ambient soil temperature above 20C: derate using the square root of (90 - Tamb)/(90 - 20). Soil thermal resistivity above 90 C-cm/W: increases T3. Multiple cables in the same trench: mutual heating reduces ampacity by 10-30% depending on spacing (use the Kennelly formula or IEC 60287 grouping factors). Depth of burial: deeper cables have worse heat dissipation. Duct bank installations have higher thermal resistance than direct burial.

Specify the cable accessories. Joints (straight joints for cable lengths exceeding shipping length, typically 500-1000m): the joint must have equal or better insulation integrity than the cable. Terminations: outdoor or GIS terminations with stress cones to manage the electric field at the insulation screen cutback. Both joints and terminations are the most common failure points in cable systems; specify factory-tested, pre-molded components and require installer certification.

steps.description: Assess the condition of power transformers using dissolved gas analysis, electrical tests, and physical inspection to make maintenance and replacement decisions.

inputs.name: cable-specification
inputs.desc: System context for transformer loading and protection

inputs.name: ampacity-calculation
inputs.desc: Loading conditions that affect transformer thermal aging

outputs.name: condition-assessment
outputs.desc: Overall transformer health index based on DGA, electrical tests, and physical inspection, with remaining life estimate

outputs.name: maintenance-recommendations
outputs.desc: Prioritized maintenance actions: oil processing, leak repair, bushing replacement, load management, or planned replacement

process: Perform dissolved gas analysis (DGA). Sample the insulating oil and measure dissolved gases: hydrogen (H2), methane (CH4), ethane (C2H6), ethylene (C2H4), acetylene (C2H2), carbon monoxide (CO), and carbon dioxide (CO2). Each gas indicates a specific fault type: H2 indicates partial discharge; C2H2 indicates arcing; C2H4 indicates high-temperature oil overheating; CO indicates cellulose degradation. Use the Duval Triangle, Rogers ratios, or IEC 60599 key gas method to classify the fault type. Trending is as important as absolute values: rapidly increasing gas levels indicate an active fault.

Perform electrical tests. Power factor (dissipation factor) test at 10kV: measures the dielectric losses in the insulation system. Values above 1% for oil-filled transformers indicate insulation degradation. Winding resistance: detects loose connections, broken strands, and tap changer contact problems. Compare phases and compare to nameplate or factory test values; differences above 2% warrant investigation. Turns ratio test: verify at all tap positions; deviation above 0.5% from nameplate indicates winding damage.

Perform frequency response analysis (FRA). Sweep a low-voltage signal across a frequency range (20Hz to 2MHz) and measure the transfer function between terminals. Compare the measured response to a baseline (factory test or previous measurement). Deviations indicate mechanical changes: winding displacement, core movement, or clamping looseness. FRA is the most sensitive test for detecting mechanical damage from through-faults or transportation incidents.

Assess insulation condition. Oil quality: measure breakdown voltage (IEC 60156, minimum 30kV for new oil, 20kV for service-aged), moisture content (Karl Fischer, less than 20ppm for transformers above 69kV), and acidity (neutralization number, less than 0.2 mgKOH/g). Paper insulation condition: degree of polymerization (DP) estimated from furan compounds in oil (2-furfuraldehyde correlates inversely with DP). DP below 200 indicates end-of-life paper; replacement may be warranted.

Calculate the health index. Combine DGA results (40% weight), electrical test results (25%), oil quality (20%), and physical condition (age, loading history, external condition: 15%) into a composite score. Map the score to a condition category: Good (normal maintenance), Fair (increased monitoring), Poor (plan repair or replacement), Very Poor (imminent failure risk, limit loading). Use the health index to prioritize capital spending across the transformer fleet.

description: Design a microgrid from load characterization through generation mix optimization, energy management system design, islanding capability, and economic analysis.

steps.description: Characterize the microgrid load: critical vs non-critical classification, load profiles, power quality requirements, and reliability targets.

inputs.name: site-description
inputs.desc: Facility type, building list, process loads, and existing electrical infrastructure

inputs.name: historical-load-data
inputs.desc: 12 months minimum of interval meter data (15-minute or hourly), peak demand, energy consumption, and power factor

outputs.name: load-classification
outputs.desc: Loads classified as critical (must be served in island mode), priority (served if capacity allows), and non-critical (shed in island mode), with power demand for each category

outputs.name: load-profile-analysis
outputs.desc: Peak, average, and minimum demand by category, daily and seasonal load shapes, power factor profile, and power quality requirements

process: Classify loads by criticality. Critical loads require continuous power (life safety, data centers, refrigeration for perishables, security systems). Priority loads can tolerate brief interruptions but should be restored quickly (HVAC, lighting for occupied spaces, communications). Non-critical loads can be shed for extended periods during island mode (decorative lighting, non-essential equipment, EV charging).

Build load profiles for each category. From interval meter data, extract the hourly load shape for weekdays and weekends, by season. Identify the peak coincident demand (all categories simultaneously) and the critical-only peak demand. The ratio of critical peak to total peak determines the minimum generation capacity for island mode. Typical ratios: military base 40-60%, hospital campus 60-80%, data center 90-100%.

Characterize power quality requirements. Voltage: ANSI C84.1 Range A for continuous, Range B for occasional excursions. Frequency: 60 Hz +/- 0.5 Hz for normal, +/- 3 Hz for transient (depends on connected equipment sensitivity). Harmonics: IEEE 519 limits at the PCC. Identify any loads with special requirements: sensitive electronics (CBEMA/ITIC curve compliance), motor starting (voltage dip limits), or three-phase balance requirements.

Define reliability targets. Express as SAIDI (minutes of interruption per year) and SAIFI (number of interruptions per year) for the microgrid. A military facility may target SAIDI less than 60 minutes (99.99% availability). A commercial campus may accept SAIDI less than 500 minutes (99.9%). These targets drive the redundancy requirements for generation and switching equipment.

Estimate load growth. Project load changes over the microgrid design life (typically 20-25 years). Account for building additions, EV charging infrastructure, electrification of heating, and energy efficiency improvements. Size the microgrid infrastructure (switchgear, conductors, transformer capacity) for the projected peak, even if the initial generation is sized for current loads.

steps.description: Optimize the generation mix for the microgrid: solar, battery, diesel/gas, wind, and other DERs, balancing cost, reliability, and emissions.

inputs.name: load-classification
inputs.desc: Load categories and power demand by category

inputs.name: load-profile-analysis
inputs.desc: Hourly load profiles for dispatch optimization

outputs.name: generation-mix
outputs.desc: Optimal capacity of each generation source (solar kW, battery kWh/kW, diesel/gas kW, wind kW) with dispatch strategy

outputs.name: economic-comparison
outputs.desc: Net present cost comparison of microgrid scenarios against grid-only and diesel-only baselines

process: Define the candidate resources. Solar PV: capacity limited by available roof and ground area, production profile from the solar resource. Battery: energy (kWh) and power (kW) are independent design variables; round-trip efficiency 85-90%. Diesel or natural gas generator: dispatchable, fuel cost per kWh, maintenance cost per operating hour, emissions rate. Wind: capacity limited by site and permitting, production profile from the wind resource. Combined heat and power (CHP): if thermal loads exist, CHP improves total efficiency from 35% (electricity only) to 70-85% (electricity + heat).

Run the optimization. Use HOMER, REopt, DER-CAM, or a custom model. The objective function is typically minimum net present cost (capital + O&M + fuel - avoided grid purchases - demand charge savings). Constraints: critical load must be served for a defined islanding duration (typically 24-72 hours for resilience), emissions limits, space limits, and noise limits. The optimizer sizes each resource and determines the dispatch order.

Size the battery for the islanding requirement. During a grid outage, the battery must bridge the gap between renewable generation and critical load. For a 24-hour islanding requirement with solar: the battery must cover the nighttime critical load plus any daytime shortfall. A rough sizing: battery kWh = critical load kW x hours without solar x (1 / round-trip efficiency). Refine with an hourly simulation of the worst-case day (minimum solar, maximum critical load).

Size the diesel/gas backup for worst-case scenarios. Even with solar and battery, extended cloudy periods or equipment failures may exhaust the battery. A diesel or gas generator sized to serve the critical load provides the ultimate backup. N+1 redundancy (one more generator than needed) is standard for high-reliability applications. Fuel storage must be sized for the maximum expected outage duration (regulatory requirements may specify minimum fuel storage for hospitals, military, etc.).

Compare scenarios. Present the NPC, LCOE, payback period, and CO2 emissions for at least three scenarios: grid-only (baseline), microgrid with optimization, and microgrid with maximum renewable penetration. The optimal scenario minimizes NPC while meeting the reliability and emissions constraints. Sensitivity to utility rate escalation, fuel price, and battery cost shows the robustness of the result.

steps.description: Design the microgrid control system: energy management, islanding detection, seamless transition, black start, and power quality management in island mode.

inputs.name: generation-mix
inputs.desc: Generation sources and their control capabilities

inputs.name: economic-comparison
inputs.desc: Selected scenario configuration

outputs.name: control-system-design
outputs.desc: Microgrid controller architecture, dispatch algorithm, islanding transition sequence, and black start procedure

outputs.name: island-mode-performance
outputs.desc: Voltage and frequency regulation capability, transient response to load steps, and maximum load that can be picked up in a single step

process: Design the microgrid controller architecture. A central microgrid controller (MMC) communicates with all DERs and the point of common coupling (PCC) breaker. The MMC performs economic dispatch (minimizing operating cost while meeting load and constraints), state estimation, and islanding transition management. Communication: typically Modbus TCP or DNP3 over Ethernet, with latency requirements below 100ms for dispatch and below 20ms for protection signals.

Design the islanding transition. For planned islanding (scheduled maintenance): pre-load the DERs to match the microgrid load, then open the PCC breaker at zero current crossing. For unplanned islanding (grid fault): detect the island condition within 2 seconds (IEEE 1547), transition the grid-forming inverter or diesel generator from grid-following to grid-forming mode, and shed non-critical loads if the available generation is less than the total load. The voltage and frequency transient during transition should stay within ANSI C84.1 Range B.

Design the black start sequence. After a complete blackout (all sources offline), the black start sequence must re-energize the microgrid without relying on the utility grid. A diesel generator with black start capability (battery cranking, no external power needed) is the typical black start source. Sequence: start the diesel generator, close onto a dead bus, sequentially energize feeders and pick up critical loads in steps (each step limited to avoid frequency and voltage excursions beyond the generator's capability, typically 30-50% of rated load per step).

Design the economic dispatch algorithm. In grid-connected mode: charge the battery when renewable generation exceeds load or when grid energy is cheap (time-of-use rates), discharge when grid energy is expensive or during demand peaks (peak shaving). Prioritize renewable self-consumption to maximize savings. In island mode: dispatch generators to follow load, charge the battery from excess renewable generation, shed non-critical loads when generation is insufficient.

Verify island mode power quality. In island mode, voltage and frequency are controlled by the grid-forming source (diesel generator or battery inverter). Simulate load transients: a sudden load increase of 20-30% of the grid-forming source's rating should not cause frequency to dip below 57 Hz or voltage below 0.88 pu (ANSI C84.1 Range B limits). If transient performance is inadequate, add a flywheel, increase battery inverter rating, or implement faster load shedding.

description: Design foundations for wind turbines: geotechnical investigation, foundation type selection, structural design, and construction methodology for onshore and offshore applications.

steps.description: Plan and execute the geotechnical investigation for wind turbine foundations: borehole program, in-situ testing, laboratory testing, and geotechnical model development.

inputs.name: turbine-layout
inputs.desc: Turbine positions, tower base loads (overturning moment, vertical force, horizontal shear), and number of turbines

inputs.name: site-geology
inputs.desc: Available geological maps, prior investigation data, and terrain classification

outputs.name: geotechnical-model
outputs.desc: Soil profile at each turbine location with design soil parameters (bearing capacity, shear strength, stiffness, water table depth)

outputs.name: foundation-design-parameters
outputs.desc: Allowable bearing pressure, friction angle, cohesion, modulus of subgrade reaction, and any geotechnical hazards (expansive soils, liquefiable layers, karst)

process: Design the investigation program. At minimum, one borehole per turbine location to a depth of 1.5 times the expected foundation diameter (typically 15-25 meters for onshore). Additional boreholes at the substation and along access roads. Include SPT (standard penetration test) at 1.5m intervals, CPT (cone penetration test) for continuous profiling, and pressuremeter or dilatometer tests for stiffness measurement.

Perform laboratory testing on undisturbed samples. Classification tests (grain size, Atterberg limits, moisture content), strength tests (triaxial compression, direct shear), consolidation tests for settlement prediction, and chemical analysis (sulfate content for concrete durability). For cohesive soils, undrained shear strength from the triaxial test governs short-term bearing capacity. For granular soils, friction angle from the CPT correlation governs bearing capacity.

Develop the geotechnical model. For each turbine location, create a soil profile showing layers, soil parameters, and the water table. Determine the design bearing pressure from the bearing capacity equation: q_ult = c x Nc + q x Nq + 0.5 x gamma x B x Ngamma, with appropriate partial safety factors (typically 2.0-3.0 for gravity foundations). The bearing pressure must also satisfy settlement limits (typically 25mm total, 10mm differential between tower legs).

Identify geotechnical hazards. Expansive clay: foundation must extend below the active zone or include a void between the foundation and expansive soil. Liquefiable sand: identify by CPT or SPT, evaluate liquefaction potential using the simplified method (Boulanger and Idriss), and design for post-liquefaction settlement or improve the ground. Karst (soluble rock with voids): require additional investigation (ground-penetrating radar, probe drilling) to map void locations. Frost heave: foundation must extend below the frost line.

Deliver the geotechnical interpretive report. Present the factual data, the geotechnical model, the design parameters with their characteristic and design values (per Eurocode 7 or IEC 61400-6), and recommendations for foundation type and construction methodology. The report is a key document for the foundation design engineer and is reviewed by the wind turbine manufacturer for compatibility with their tower base loads.

steps.description: Design the structural foundation for an onshore wind turbine: gravity base or pile foundation, reinforcement design, anchor bolt embedment, and construction detailing.

inputs.name: geotechnical-model
inputs.desc: Soil profile and design parameters at the turbine location

inputs.name: foundation-design-parameters
inputs.desc: Allowable bearing pressure, stiffness, and hazard mitigation requirements

outputs.name: foundation-design
outputs.desc: Foundation type, dimensions, reinforcement layout, anchor bolt ring specification, and concrete mix design

outputs.name: construction-specification
outputs.desc: Excavation requirements, concrete placement sequence, curing requirements, backfill specification, and quality control plan

process: Select the foundation type. Gravity base (octagonal or circular pad, 15-22m diameter, 2-3m deep) is standard for onshore wind turbines on competent soil with adequate bearing capacity (greater than 150 kPa). Pile foundation (driven steel piles or drilled shafts) is used when bearing capacity is insufficient at shallow depth or when the soil is highly compressible. Rock-anchored foundations use post-tensioned anchors drilled into competent rock.

Size the gravity base foundation. The overturning moment from the tower base is resisted by the weight of the foundation and the overlying soil. Verify: bearing pressure under the combined vertical load and overturning moment does not exceed the allowable (use Meyerhof's effective area method for eccentric loading). Verify rotational stiffness meets the turbine manufacturer's requirement (typically expressed as a maximum rotation at the foundation top for the design moment).

Design the reinforcement. The foundation slab acts as a cantilevered plate loaded by the soil bearing pressure. The bending moment is maximum at the pedestal face. Design the radial and circumferential reinforcement per ACI 318 or Eurocode 2 for the factored bending moments and shear forces. Minimum reinforcement ratios apply to control cracking. The pedestal transfers the anchor bolt forces into the slab: design for the combined tension, shear, and bending from the tower base flange.

Specify the anchor bolt ring. The anchor bolt ring (typically 100-140 bolts of 36-72mm diameter arranged on a 4-5m diameter circle) transfers the tower overturning moment into the foundation as a tension-compression couple. Bolt embedment length must develop the bolt's proof load. The bolt template must be surveyed to within 1mm tolerance for compatible mating with the tower base flange.

Develop the construction specification. Excavation to design depth with proof rolling to verify bearing capacity. Lean concrete mud mat (75-100mm) for a clean working surface. Reinforcement placement with spacers for cover. Continuous concrete pour (a 500-800 cubic meter pour for a large foundation) with temperature monitoring for mass concrete effects (limit temperature rise to 20C above ambient to prevent thermal cracking). Cure for 28 days minimum before tower erection loading. Backfill with compacted select fill to restore overburden.

steps.description: Design foundations for offshore wind turbines: monopile, jacket, gravity base, or floating concepts, considering wave and current loads, soil-structure interaction, and marine construction methods.

inputs.name: foundation-design
inputs.desc: Onshore design methodology adapted for offshore loading conditions

inputs.name: construction-specification
inputs.desc: Construction methods adapted for marine installation

outputs.name: offshore-foundation-design
outputs.desc: Foundation type, dimensions, wall thickness, grouted connection or bolted connection design, and scour protection

outputs.name: installation-methodology
outputs.desc: Vessel requirements, installation sequence, pile driving or suction installation parameters, and weather window requirements

process: Select the foundation type by water depth. Monopile: 0-40m water depth (single large-diameter steel pipe, 6-10m diameter, driven 20-40m into the seabed). Jacket: 25-65m (lattice steel structure with 3-4 pin piles). Gravity base: 0-30m (massive concrete or steel structure relying on weight, suitable for hard seabed). Floating (spar, semi-sub, TLP): beyond 60m depth. Monopiles account for over 80% of installed offshore wind foundations due to their simplicity.

Design for hydrodynamic loads. Wave loads on the monopile are calculated from Morison's equation: F = 0.5 x Cd x rho x D x |u| x u + Cm x rho x pi x D2/4 x du/dt (drag + inertia). For large-diameter monopiles (D/wavelength greater than 0.2), diffraction effects require the MacCamy-Fuchs correction. Current loads add a steady drag force. Wave and current loads are combined with wind loads for the design load cases per IEC 61400-3 (offshore wind standard).

Analyze soil-structure interaction. The monopile is a laterally loaded pile. Model the soil-pile interaction using p-y curves (API RP 2GEO or DNVGL-RP-C212). The p-y method provides the lateral soil resistance as a function of lateral displacement at each depth. For clay: use the Matlock soft clay or Reese stiff clay p-y curves. For sand: use the API sand p-y curves. The natural frequency of the monopile-tower system must fall between the 1P and 3P frequencies (the soft-stiff design range) to avoid resonance with rotor excitation.

Design the grouted or bolted connection. The transition piece connects the monopile to the tower. A grouted connection uses high-strength grout to transfer loads between the transition piece and the monopile. The grout must resist the combination of axial force, bending, and shear. Shear keys (welded ribs on both the inside of the transition piece and outside of the monopile) provide mechanical interlock. Alternatively, a bolted flange connection avoids grout but requires precise pile installation tolerances.

Design scour protection. Currents and waves cause scouring of the seabed around the monopile, potentially reducing the embedment depth and lateral capacity. Scour depth for a cylindrical monopile in current is approximately 1.3 x D (pile diameter). Rock armor (graded rock placed around the pile base) or concrete mattresses prevent scour. The rock armor layer is typically 0.5-1.0m thick with a D50 stone size calculated from the current velocity using the Isbash or Hudson formula.

description: Design protection systems for microgrids with bidirectional power flow, variable fault current sources, and the need to operate in both grid-connected and island modes.

steps.description: Characterize fault currents in the microgrid for both grid-connected and island modes, accounting for the different fault current contributions of inverter-based and rotating DERs.

inputs.name: microgrid-configuration
inputs.desc: Single-line diagram with all DER sources, their fault current characteristics, and the PCC configuration

inputs.name: protection-requirements
inputs.desc: Reliability targets, selectivity requirements, and regulatory obligations

outputs.name: fault-current-analysis
outputs.desc: Maximum and minimum fault currents at each bus in grid-connected and island mode, with the contributing sources identified

outputs.name: protection-challenges
outputs.desc: Identified challenges: reduced fault current in island mode, bidirectional flow, and variable source impedance

process: Calculate fault currents in grid-connected mode. The utility source provides the dominant fault current contribution (typically 5-20 kA at the medium-voltage PCC). Inverter-based DERs contribute 1.1-1.2 times rated current. Diesel generators contribute 3-5 times rated current (subtransient). Sum contributions at each bus using superposition.

Calculate fault currents in island mode. Without the utility source, fault current drops dramatically. If the microgrid has only inverter-based DERs, the maximum fault current may be only 1.2 times the total rated current of all online inverters. This is often insufficient to operate conventional overcurrent relays. If diesel generators are the grid-forming sources, fault current is 3-5 times generator rating, providing more margin for conventional protection.

Identify the fault current ratio. The ratio of grid-connected to island mode fault current at each bus determines the protection challenge. Ratios of 5:1 to 20:1 are common. Conventional overcurrent relays set for grid-connected faults may not pick up island mode faults. Conversely, relays set for island mode faults may trip on normal load current in grid-connected mode.

Characterize the time-varying nature. In island mode, as DERs trip on fault detection, the fault current decreases further. Inverters may limit current to 1.1 pu after 1-2 cycles. Diesel generators provide decaying fault current (subtransient to transient to steady-state) over 0.1-5 seconds. The protection system must be coordinated with these time-varying contributions.

Map the bidirectional flow paths. Unlike radial distribution, a microgrid may have loop topology or multiple sources feeding a bus from different directions. Faults can be fed from multiple directions simultaneously. This requires directional protection elements to determine which section is faulted and avoid tripping healthy sections.

steps.description: Design an adaptive protection scheme that adjusts relay settings between grid-connected and island mode to maintain selectivity and sensitivity under varying fault current conditions.

inputs.name: fault-current-analysis
inputs.desc: Fault currents in both operating modes

inputs.name: protection-challenges
inputs.desc: Specific challenges requiring adaptive solutions

outputs.name: adaptive-protection-scheme
outputs.desc: Relay selection, dual setting groups, mode-switching logic, and communication architecture for adaptive protection

outputs.name: protection-coordination-results
outputs.desc: Time-current coordination plots for both grid-connected and island mode, showing selectivity and sensitivity at all fault current levels

process: Select relays with dual setting groups. Modern numerical relays (SEL, ABB, Siemens, GE) support multiple setting groups that can be switched by a digital input or communication command. Define Setting Group 1 for grid-connected mode (higher pickup, conventional coordination) and Setting Group 2 for island mode (lower pickup, faster clearing times).

Set the grid-connected group (Group 1). Follow conventional coordination practices: 51 pickup above maximum load, coordinated with upstream utility relays (the utility provides coordination requirements in the interconnection agreement). Instantaneous (50) elements set above maximum through-fault current from downstream sources.

Set the island mode group (Group 2). Lower the 51 pickup to detect the reduced island-mode fault currents. This may require pickup as low as 1.5-2.0 times rated load current, which leaves little margin for normal load variation. Use definite-time overcurrent with fast tripping (0.1-0.3 seconds) rather than inverse-time curves, since the reduced fault current provides less discrimination margin. Add negative-sequence overcurrent (46) elements that are more sensitive to fault current than phase overcurrent when fault current is near load current magnitude.

Design the mode-switching logic. The microgrid controller detects the transition between grid-connected and island mode (from the PCC breaker status) and sends a command to switch all relay setting groups. Communication latency must be less than the fastest relay operating time to prevent misoperation during the transition. Hardwired (digital inputs from PCC breaker auxiliary contacts) is faster and more reliable than communication-based switching.

Add communication-based protection for enhanced selectivity. Directional comparison blocking or permissive schemes (similar to transmission line pilot protection) use fiber or Ethernet communication between relays to achieve selectivity without time coordination delays. If relay A detects a fault in the forward direction and relay B does not detect a fault in the reverse direction, relay A trips. This provides fast, selective clearing regardless of the fault current level.
